title: PLAN: Database Preprocessing — Building openLCA Databases Without the Desktop App
text:
How to build a pre-processed openLCA database (equivalent to what the openLCA desktop app produces) using only Python and the gdt-server REST API, then store it for fast reuse in GitHub releases. This approach replaces the need for the openLCA desktop application entirely.




The gdt-server is a calculation engine, not a database builder. It expects to be pointed at a pre-built Apache Derby database folder. The standard way to build that database is to use the openLCA desktop app — import a data pack, and the app writes the Derby database to disk.
The problem: openLCA desktop is a 500MB GUI application. In a Codespace or CI environment, you do not want to install a GUI app just to build a database.
The solution discovered in this project: the desktop app’s import logic is available in the open-source olca-modules Java library, which is also embedded inside gdt-server. The gdt-server REST API exposes enough of that logic to replicate the full import — if you import entities in the right order.




The gdt-server’s ImpactCategoryReader resolves each impact factor’s flow by UUID at import time. If the flow does not exist in the database when the ImpactCategory is PUT, the factor is silently dropped and the LCIA score for that flow becomes zero.
Correct import order: 1. UnitGroup — unit systems (Mass, Energy, Volume, etc.) 2. FlowProperty — physical quantities (kg, kWh, m³, etc.) 3. Flow — elementary flows (CO₂, NOx, SO₂, etc.) that impact factors reference 4. ImpactCategory — the scoring rules, each referencing flows by UUID 5. ImpactMethod — groups of categories into a named method (TRACI 2.2, ReCiPe, etc.)
This is exactly the order the openLCA desktop app uses internally.




Located at the project root. Streams each entity type from the source zip in a separate pass so only one type is in memory at a time (avoids OOM on the 60,000+ flow entries).
Source zip (JSON-LD format)
    │
    ├─ Pass 1: UnitGroup     (~10 entities)    → PUT /data/unit-group
    ├─ Pass 2: FlowProperty  (~10 entities)    → PUT /data/flow-property
    ├─ Pass 3: Flow          (~60,000 entities) → PUT /data/flow
    ├─ Pass 4: ImpactCategory (~550 entities)  → PUT /data/impact-category
    └─ Pass 5: ImpactMethod  (~45 entities)    → PUT /data/impact-method
                                                        │
                                               gdt-server writes to
                                               Apache Derby database
                                               ~/olca-data/databases/lca_methods/
After all passes complete, the Derby database folder is a fully functional pre-built database identical to what the desktop app would have produced.




This is the easiest thing to get wrong and the hardest to diagnose because gdt-server fails silently.
When setup_olca.sh starts the server with -db lca_methods, gdt-server looks for ~/olca-data/databases/lca_methods/. If that folder does not exist, it silently creates a new empty database at that path. No error. No warning. The server starts fine and responds to API calls — but every query returns zero results.
The tar archive must therefore contain the database folder under the name lca_methods/ (not lca_commons/ or any other name). Always verify this before uploading:
# Check what folder name is inside the archive — must print "lca_methods/"
tar -tzf ~/olca-data/lca_methods-LCIA-methods-2.8.0-2026-06-18.tar.gz | head -1
The setup_olca.sh guard condition must also use the same name:
# In setup_olca.sh — these three names must all match:
LCA_COMMONS_DB="$DATA_DIR/databases/lca_methods"   # ← the check
tar -xzf ...                                         # ← extracts lca_methods/ from archive
docker run ... -db lca_methods                       # ← the server flag
If any of them differ, a new Codespace will silently get an empty database.
History: In June 2026, the database was renamed from lca_commons to lca_methods throughout the scripts, but the tar.gz on GitHub releases was rebuilt from an empty database (not the correctly-populated one). The result: every new Codespace had 0 LCIA methods. The fix was to re-run the import, tar with the correct folder name, and re-upload.




This workflow runs once per database. After it completes, the database is stored in GitHub releases and never rebuilt unless the source data changes.
1. Start gdt-server pointed at an empty database named lca_methods
      docker rm -f olca-server
      docker run --name olca-server --network host \
          -v "$HOME/olca-data:/app/data" -d gdt-server:latest -db lca_methods
      # Wait for it to start: curl -s http://localhost:8080/api/version

2. Download the source zip from GitHub releases
      gh release download lca-data-v1 \
          --repo calvinw/agentic-lca \
          --pattern "openLCA.LCIA.Methods.*.zip" \
          --output "$HOME/olca-data/openLCA_LCIA_methods.zip"

3. Run the preprocessing script
      python3 import_lca_data.py
      # Takes ~20-30 minutes (60,000 flows is the slow pass)
      # If interrupted, see "Recovering from a partial import" below

4. Verify the database before tarballing
      python3 -c "
      from olca_ipc.rest import RestClient; import olca_schema as o
      c = RestClient('http://localhost:8080/')
      methods = list(c.get_descriptors(o.ImpactMethod))
      print(f'Methods: {len(methods)}')   # must be 45
      traci = [m.name for m in methods if 'traci' in (m.name or '').lower()]
      print(f'TRACI: {traci}')            # must include TRACI 2.2
      "

5. Stop the server cleanly before tarballing
      docker stop olca-server

6. Create the archive — folder name inside MUST be lca_methods/
      tar -czf ~/olca-data/lca_methods-LCIA-methods-2.8.0-$(date +%Y-%m-%d).tar.gz \
          -C ~/olca-data/databases lca_methods/

      # Verify the folder name inside the archive before uploading:
      tar -tzf ~/olca-data/lca_methods-LCIA-methods-*.tar.gz | head -1
      # Must print: lca_methods/

7. Upload to GitHub releases (--clobber replaces an existing file of the same name)
      gh release upload lca-data-v1 \
          ~/olca-data/lca_methods-LCIA-methods-*.tar.gz \
          --repo calvinw/agentic-lca --clobber
After step 7, all future Codespace sessions just download and unzip the pre-built database. The import step never runs again unless the source data changes.




The import can be interrupted mid-run (e.g. Codespace idle timeout during the 60,000-flow pass). The database is not corrupted — you can check what made it in and run only the missing passes.
# Check what's already in the database
from olca_ipc.rest import RestClient; import olca_schema as o
c = RestClient('http://localhost:8080/')
print(len(list(c.get_descriptors(o.Flow))))           # expect ~60,914
print(len(list(c.get_descriptors(o.ImpactCategory)))) # expect ~480 (550 in some packs)
print(len(list(c.get_descriptors(o.ImpactMethod))))   # expect 45
If flows and categories are in but methods are missing (the most likely interruption point since it is the last pass), run only the ImpactMethod pass:
import json, zipfile
from pathlib import Path
from olca_ipc.rest import RestClient; import olca_schema as o

PACK = Path.home() / "olca-data/openLCA_LCIA_methods.zip"
client = RestClient("http://localhost:8080/")
ok = total = 0
with zipfile.ZipFile(PACK) as zf:
    for name in zf.namelist():
        if not name.endswith(".json"): continue
        try:
            raw = json.loads(zf.read(name))
            items = raw if isinstance(raw, list) else \
                    raw.get("@graph", []) if "@graph" in raw else \
                    [raw] if "@type" in raw else []
            for item in items:
                if item.get("@type") == "ImpactMethod":
                    total += 1
                    if client.put(o.ImpactMethod.from_dict(item)):
                        ok += 1; print(f"  ✓ {item.get('name')}")
        except Exception: pass
print(f"Imported {ok}/{total} ImpactMethods")
Then continue from step 4 (verify) in the build workflow above.

Contents
Used by

Pre-built Derby DB — 45 LCIA methods, 60,914 flows, 480 impact categories. Folder inside archive: lca_methods/

The methods pack zip is no longer downloaded by setup_olca.sh but is kept in the release as the source material for rebuilding the tar.gz if needed (e.g. when a newer methods pack version is released).
Naming convention for the tar.gz: include the methods pack version and build date so it is clear which source was used: lca_methods-LCIA-methods-{pack-version}-{build-date}.tar.gz




The same pattern applies to any openLCA-compatible database.


BAFU 2025 — 11,747 Swiss background processes, free download, EF 3.1 compatible
Source: bafu2025.zip from bafu.admin.ch (free)

Build:
  1. Start gdt-server with empty `bafu` database (-db bafu)
  2. python3 import_lca_data.py --source bafu2025.zip --db bafu
     Import order: UnitGroup → FlowProperty → Flow → Process → ImpactCategory → ImpactMethod
  3. tar -czf bafu.tar.gz -C ~/olca-data/databases bafu/
  4. gh release upload lca-data-v1 bafu.tar.gz --repo calvinw/agentic-lca

Setup script addition:
  if [ ! -d "$DATA_DIR/databases/bafu" ]; then
      curl -L "$RELEASE_BASE/bafu.tar.gz" | tar -xz -C "$DATA_DIR/databases/"
  fi
  docker run ... -db bafu
BAFU pairs naturally with EF 3.1 Method (adapted) which is already loaded in lca_methods. If using lca_methods as the base database, BAFU processes can be imported on top of it.



ecoinvent — industry-standard, requires license from ecoinvent.org
ecoinvent is distributed as a .zolca file (openLCA’s native export format). This format is not a JSON-LD zip — it is a compressed Derby database snapshot.
Build (on a machine with the ecoinvent license):
  Option A — openLCA desktop app:
    1. Open openLCA desktop
    2. File → Import → .zolca file
    3. Close openLCA
    4. tar -czf ecoinvent.tar.gz -C ~/openLCA-data-1.4/databases ecoinvent/

  Option B — programmatic (if .zolca unpacks to JSON-LD):
    unzip ecoinvent.zolca -d ecoinvent_jsonld/
    python3 import_lca_data.py --source ecoinvent_jsonld/ --db ecoinvent
    tar -czf ecoinvent.tar.gz -C ~/olca-data/databases ecoinvent/

Storage:
  gh release create lca-data-v1 ecoinvent.tar.gz \
      --repo calvinw/ecoinvent-lca-db   ← private repository
Download in Codespace (authenticated via built-in GitHub token or Codespaces secret):
gh release download lca-data-v1 \
    --repo calvinw/ecoinvent-lca-db \
    --pattern "ecoinvent.tar.gz" \
    --output "$DATA_DIR/ecoinvent.tar.gz"
tar -xzf "$DATA_DIR/ecoinvent.tar.gz" -C "$DATA_DIR/databases/"

text:
The gdt-server’s ImpactCategoryReader resolves each impact factor’s flow by UUID at import time. If the flow does not exist in the database when the ImpactCategory is PUT, the factor is silently dropped and the LCIA score for that flow becomes zero.
Correct import order: 1. UnitGroup — unit systems (Mass, Energy, Volume, etc.) 2. FlowProperty — physical quantities (kg, kWh, m³, etc.) 3. Flow — elementary flows (CO₂, NOx, SO₂, etc.) that impact factors reference 4. ImpactCategory — the scoring rules, each referencing flows by UUID 5. ImpactMethod — groups of categories into a named method (TRACI 2.2, ReCiPe, etc.)
This is exactly the order the openLCA desktop app uses internally.

title: PLAN: Database Preprocessing — Building openLCA Databases Without the Desktop App
text:
Located at the project root. Streams each entity type from the source zip in a separate pass so only one type is in memory at a time (avoids OOM on the 60,000+ flow entries).
Source zip (JSON-LD format)
    │
    ├─ Pass 1: UnitGroup     (~10 entities)    → PUT /data/unit-group
    ├─ Pass 2: FlowProperty  (~10 entities)    → PUT /data/flow-property
    ├─ Pass 3: Flow          (~60,000 entities) → PUT /data/flow
    ├─ Pass 4: ImpactCategory (~550 entities)  → PUT /data/impact-category
    └─ Pass 5: ImpactMethod  (~45 entities)    → PUT /data/impact-method
                                                        │
                                               gdt-server writes to
                                               Apache Derby database
                                               ~/olca-data/databases/lca_methods/
After all passes complete, the Derby database folder is a fully functional pre-built database identical to what the desktop app would have produced.

title: PLAN: Database Preprocessing — Building openLCA Databases Without the Desktop App
text:
This is the easiest thing to get wrong and the hardest to diagnose because gdt-server fails silently.
When setup_olca.sh starts the server with -db lca_methods, gdt-server looks for ~/olca-data/databases/lca_methods/. If that folder does not exist, it silently creates a new empty database at that path. No error. No warning. The server starts fine and responds to API calls — but every query returns zero results.
The tar archive must therefore contain the database folder under the name lca_methods/ (not lca_commons/ or any other name). Always verify this before uploading:
# Check what folder name is inside the archive — must print "lca_methods/"
tar -tzf ~/olca-data/lca_methods-LCIA-methods-2.8.0-2026-06-18.tar.gz | head -1
The setup_olca.sh guard condition must also use the same name:
# In setup_olca.sh — these three names must all match:
LCA_COMMONS_DB="$DATA_DIR/databases/lca_methods"   # ← the check
tar -xzf ...                                         # ← extracts lca_methods/ from archive
docker run ... -db lca_methods                       # ← the server flag
If any of them differ, a new Codespace will silently get an empty database.
History: In June 2026, the database was renamed from lca_commons to lca_methods throughout the scripts, but the tar.gz on GitHub releases was rebuilt from an empty database (not the correctly-populated one). The result: every new Codespace had 0 LCIA methods. The fix was to re-run the import, tar with the correct folder name, and re-upload.

title: PLAN: Database Preprocessing — Building openLCA Databases Without the Desktop App
text:
This workflow runs once per database. After it completes, the database is stored in GitHub releases and never rebuilt unless the source data changes.
1. Start gdt-server pointed at an empty database named lca_methods
      docker rm -f olca-server
      docker run --name olca-server --network host \
          -v "$HOME/olca-data:/app/data" -d gdt-server:latest -db lca_methods
      # Wait for it to start: curl -s http://localhost:8080/api/version

2. Download the source zip from GitHub releases
      gh release download lca-data-v1 \
          --repo calvinw/agentic-lca \
          --pattern "openLCA.LCIA.Methods.*.zip" \
          --output "$HOME/olca-data/openLCA_LCIA_methods.zip"

3. Run the preprocessing script
      python3 import_lca_data.py
      # Takes ~20-30 minutes (60,000 flows is the slow pass)
      # If interrupted, see "Recovering from a partial import" below

4. Verify the database before tarballing
      python3 -c "
      from olca_ipc.rest import RestClient; import olca_schema as o
      c = RestClient('http://localhost:8080/')
      methods = list(c.get_descriptors(o.ImpactMethod))
      print(f'Methods: {len(methods)}')   # must be 45
      traci = [m.name for m in methods if 'traci' in (m.name or '').lower()]
      print(f'TRACI: {traci}')            # must include TRACI 2.2
      "

5. Stop the server cleanly before tarballing
      docker stop olca-server

6. Create the archive — folder name inside MUST be lca_methods/
      tar -czf ~/olca-data/lca_methods-LCIA-methods-2.8.0-$(date +%Y-%m-%d).tar.gz \
          -C ~/olca-data/databases lca_methods/

      # Verify the folder name inside the archive before uploading:
      tar -tzf ~/olca-data/lca_methods-LCIA-methods-*.tar.gz | head -1
      # Must print: lca_methods/

7. Upload to GitHub releases (--clobber replaces an existing file of the same name)
      gh release upload lca-data-v1 \
          ~/olca-data/lca_methods-LCIA-methods-*.tar.gz \
          --repo calvinw/agentic-lca --clobber
After step 7, all future Codespace sessions just download and unzip the pre-built database. The import step never runs again unless the source data changes.

title: PLAN: Database Preprocessing — Building openLCA Databases Without the Desktop App
text:
The import can be interrupted mid-run (e.g. Codespace idle timeout during the 60,000-flow pass). The database is not corrupted — you can check what made it in and run only the missing passes.
# Check what's already in the database
from olca_ipc.rest import RestClient; import olca_schema as o
c = RestClient('http://localhost:8080/')
print(len(list(c.get_descriptors(o.Flow))))           # expect ~60,914
print(len(list(c.get_descriptors(o.ImpactCategory)))) # expect ~480 (550 in some packs)
print(len(list(c.get_descriptors(o.ImpactMethod))))   # expect 45
If flows and categories are in but methods are missing (the most likely interruption point since it is the last pass), run only the ImpactMethod pass:
import json, zipfile
from pathlib import Path
from olca_ipc.rest import RestClient; import olca_schema as o

PACK = Path.home() / "olca-data/openLCA_LCIA_methods.zip"
client = RestClient("http://localhost:8080/")
ok = total = 0
with zipfile.ZipFile(PACK) as zf:
    for name in zf.namelist():
        if not name.endswith(".json"): continue
        try:
            raw = json.loads(zf.read(name))
            items = raw if isinstance(raw, list) else \
                    raw.get("@graph", []) if "@graph" in raw else \
                    [raw] if "@type" in raw else []
            for item in items:
                if item.get("@type") == "ImpactMethod":
                    total += 1
                    if client.put(o.ImpactMethod.from_dict(item)):
                        ok += 1; print(f"  ✓ {item.get('name')}")
        except Exception: pass
print(f"Imported {ok}/{total} ImpactMethods")
Then continue from step 4 (verify) in the build workflow above.

title: PLAN: Database Preprocessing — Building openLCA Databases Without the Desktop App
text:
The same pattern applies to any openLCA-compatible database.


BAFU 2025 — 11,747 Swiss background processes, free download, EF 3.1 compatible
Source: bafu2025.zip from bafu.admin.ch (free)

Build:
  1. Start gdt-server with empty `bafu` database (-db bafu)
  2. python3 import_lca_data.py --source bafu2025.zip --db bafu
     Import order: UnitGroup → FlowProperty → Flow → Process → ImpactCategory → ImpactMethod
  3. tar -czf bafu.tar.gz -C ~/olca-data/databases bafu/
  4. gh release upload lca-data-v1 bafu.tar.gz --repo calvinw/agentic-lca

Setup script addition:
  if [ ! -d "$DATA_DIR/databases/bafu" ]; then
      curl -L "$RELEASE_BASE/bafu.tar.gz" | tar -xz -C "$DATA_DIR/databases/"
  fi
  docker run ... -db bafu
BAFU pairs naturally with EF 3.1 Method (adapted) which is already loaded in lca_methods. If using lca_methods as the base database, BAFU processes can be imported on top of it.



ecoinvent — industry-standard, requires license from ecoinvent.org
ecoinvent is distributed as a .zolca file (openLCA’s native export format). This format is not a JSON-LD zip — it is a compressed Derby database snapshot.
Build (on a machine with the ecoinvent license):
  Option A — openLCA desktop app:
    1. Open openLCA desktop
    2. File → Import → .zolca file
    3. Close openLCA
    4. tar -czf ecoinvent.tar.gz -C ~/openLCA-data-1.4/databases ecoinvent/

  Option B — programmatic (if .zolca unpacks to JSON-LD):
    unzip ecoinvent.zolca -d ecoinvent_jsonld/
    python3 import_lca_data.py --source ecoinvent_jsonld/ --db ecoinvent
    tar -czf ecoinvent.tar.gz -C ~/olca-data/databases ecoinvent/

Storage:
  gh release create lca-data-v1 ecoinvent.tar.gz \
      --repo calvinw/ecoinvent-lca-db   ← private repository
Download in Codespace (authenticated via built-in GitHub token or Codespaces secret):
gh release download lca-data-v1 \
    --repo calvinw/ecoinvent-lca-db \
    --pattern "ecoinvent.tar.gz" \
    --output "$DATA_DIR/ecoinvent.tar.gz"
tar -xzf "$DATA_DIR/ecoinvent.tar.gz" -C "$DATA_DIR/databases/"

title: /what-is-lca
text:
/what-is-lca
Skill version: 0.1 Student: calvinw Model: gpt-5.6-sol Date: 2026-07-10

AI: Imagine a cotton T-shirt and a polyester T-shirt are on your desk. One colleague says cotton is more sustainable because it is natural; another says polyester is better because it lasts longer.
Who do you think is right—and how could we fairly find out?
Student: dont we have to find a common way to compare them
AI: Exactly—that instinct is the beginning of the LCA mindset. We need a common, fair basis for comparison, such as “providing one wearable T-shirt for 100 wears,” and then examine the same environmental effects across both products.
LCA stands for Life Cycle Assessment. Think of it as a receipt showing a product’s hidden environmental costs—CO₂ emissions, water use, and pollution—from raw materials through production, use, and disposal.
Which impacts would you want that comparison to include?
Student: all of those and maybe more
AI: Exactly. A fair comparison might include climate emissions, water use, land use, energy demand, chemical pollution, and waste—because a shirt can perform well in one area but poorly in another.
For fashion buyers and designers, LCA helps replace a vague “sustainable” hangtag with evidence and reveals where improvements would matter most. Why might comparing only carbon emissions give you a misleading answer?
Student: since there are other considerations
AI: Exactly. A cotton shirt might have lower carbon emissions but require much more water, while a polyester shirt might use less water but depend on fossil fuels and release microfibers. LCA keeps us from calling something “better” after looking at only one environmental issue.
The first phase is goal and scope: decide why you are comparing the shirts and draw a fence around what the study will include. Where do you think that fence should end—at the factory, after customer use, or at disposal?
Student: can you stop the skill
AI: Sure—the what-is-lca lesson is stopped. We can continue normally whenever you’re ready.

Student: use calvinw

title: /technosphere-and-ecosphere wool_yarn
text:
/technosphere-and-ecosphere wool_yarn
Skill version: 0.1 Student: elena Model: sonnet-4-6 Date: 2026-06-15

AI: Imagine a busy town that has a wall around it. Inside the wall: houses, factories, shops, roads — everything built and run by people. Outside the wall: fields, rivers, the sky, the forest — nature, exactly as it would be without humans.
Now imagine a factory inside the wall burns coal to run its machines. Two things happen: first, a truck drives through the town and delivers the coal (that coal never leaves the wall — it moves from one part of the human world to another). Second, the chimney sends smoke up into the sky above the wall — and that smoke drifts out beyond the wall into the fields and the river.
Here is the question: which of those two things — the coal truck or the chimney smoke — actually crosses the wall and reaches the natural world outside?
Student: chimney smoke
AI: Exactly — the coal truck stayed inside the town the whole time. It moved from a coal yard to a factory, but it never left the human-made world. The chimney smoke is the one that crossed the wall and drifted out into the fields and the river. That crossing is where environmental harm begins.
In Life Cycle Assessment, researchers use two names for these two worlds. The human-made world — everything inside the wall, like factories, farms, mills, and trucks — is called the technosphere (from “techno”, meaning made by people). The natural world outside the wall — air, water, soil, living ecosystems — is called the ecosphere (from “eco”, meaning the living environment).
The most important idea in LCA is this: environmental harm only happens when something crosses the boundary between the two. Emissions released into the ecosphere (like CO₂ into the air) and resources pulled out of the ecosphere (like water from a river) are the flows that cause impact. Everything that moves around inside the technosphere — a bag of raw wool travelling from a farm to a mill, say — stays inside the wall and does not directly harm the natural world.
Now let’s sort a real LCA study into these two worlds. This is the product graph for Wool Yarn — 1 kg.
 ../../skills_references/wool_yarn/product_graph_structure.svg
Inside the wall — the technosphere: The two boxes in this diagram are the processes — the human activities that make the yarn. In this study that means Sheep farming and Wool yarn production. Also inside the wall is the intermediate product flowing between those two boxes: Raw wool passing from the farm to the mill. That flow stays entirely inside the human-made world. It does not touch nature.
Crossing the wall — into and out of the ecosphere: Two types of flows cross the boundary in this study: - Emissions going out into nature: Carbon dioxide and Methane, both released to air. These are substances the processes produce and discharge into the natural world. - Resources coming in from nature: Water, drawn from a natural water source to run the scouring and spinning operations.
In LCA, these crossings are called elementary flows — elementary because they are the basic exchanges between the human world and the natural world. They are the only flows that score as environmental impact, because they are the only ones that actually reach the ecosphere.
Looking at those two emissions — Carbon dioxide and Methane — which one do you think causes more harm to the climate? Take a guess — there is no wrong answer here.
Student: carbon dioxide
AI: That is a very reasonable guess — carbon dioxide is the gas we hear about most often in climate discussions, so it feels like the obvious answer. And this study does emit more CO₂ by weight than methane: 2.5 kg of CO₂ compared to 0.4 kg of methane from the sheep farm.
But here is the surprising part: methane is actually the bigger climate problem in this study. Scientists have measured how powerfully each gas traps heat, and it turns out that one kilogram of methane traps about 28 times as much heat as one kilogram of CO₂. That methane comes from the sheep themselves — it is released during digestion, a process called enteric fermentation. The sheep burp and exhale it constantly, and every kilogram crosses the wall from the technosphere straight into the ecosphere.
So here is the what-if question: if the sheep farm stopped emitting methane entirely — same coal burned, same water used, same CO₂ released — but the methane crossing disappeared completely, how much of the total climate impact do you think would vanish? More than half, or less than half?
Student: more than half
AI: You are exactly right — and the actual number is striking. Once you apply that 28× multiplier to the methane, the maths looks like this:

Methane from the sheep farm: 0.44 kg × 28 = 12.3 kg CO₂ equivalent
Carbon dioxide from the farm: 0.55 kg CO₂ equivalent
Carbon dioxide from the mill: 2.0 kg CO₂ equivalent
Total: roughly 14.9 kg CO₂ equivalent per kilogram of wool yarn

The methane alone accounts for about 83% of the total climate impact — even though it looked like the smaller number on the page. Remove it, and nearly the entire footprint disappears. This is exactly why the ecosphere crossing matters more than the raw weight: a small amount of a potent gas crossing the wall can dwarf everything else in the study.
This has a direct lesson for anyone buying or sourcing wool. A supplier who focuses on reducing energy use at the mill — cutting the CO₂ from scouring and spinning — is tackling only 14% of the problem. The real hotspot is the sheep farm, and the real culprit is a gas that comes from the animals themselves. That is not easy to fix, but knowing where the crossing happens is the only way to know where to act.
The technosphere-ecosphere boundary is the reason LCA studies track elementary flows — that is the official name for the crossings we have been talking about. The next natural step is understanding how those flows get converted into impact scores — a process called characterisation, which is where that 28× multiplier actually comes from. Would you like to explore that, or is there anything about the two worlds you would like to look at more closely?

title: /system-boundary wool_yarn
text:
/system-boundary wool_yarn
Skill version: 0.1 Student: calvin Model: sonnet-4-6 Date: 2026-06-14

AI: Imagine you are reviewing a restaurant receipt at the end of a work dinner. The receipt only shows the food and drinks your table ordered — it does not include the taxi you took to get there, the parking fee your colleague paid, or the round of drinks someone bought at the bar next door.
Here’s the question: if someone added up only the restaurant receipt to figure out the total cost of the evening, would that number be accurate — and what would be missing from it?
Student: taxi parking, it would not be accurate
AI: Exactly — the receipt only covers what happened inside that restaurant. Everything else, no matter how real and costly it was, simply does not appear on it.
In Life Cycle Assessment, every study has a “receipt” too — a defined set of steps it covers and a defined set it does not. That boundary is called the system boundary. Think of it as a fence drawn around part of the supply chain. Everything inside the fence is measured and counted. Everything outside the fence is ignored — even if it causes real environmental harm.
The system boundary is not a flaw — it is a deliberate choice. But it means the number you get at the end of a study only tells you about what was inside the fence.
Let’s look at a real example — a study of Wool Yarn. The goal is to calculate the climate impact of producing 1 kg of wool yarn, tracing the supply chain from sheep farming through to the spinning mill.
Here is the supply chain diagram for this study:
 ../../skills_references/wool_yarn/product_graph_structure.svg
Each box in this diagram is a step the study decided to include. The fence — the system boundary — runs around both of these boxes. Any step that does not appear is outside the fence and was not counted.
Looking at the diagram, can you spot any steps you might expect to be there that are not shown? For example — is there anything that happens to the yarn after it leaves the spinning mill that might also cause environmental impact?
Student: yes, it gets washed or used
AI: You are asking exactly the right thing — and yes, you’ve spotted something real.
After the yarn leaves the spinning mill, it gets transported to a garment factory, knitted or woven into a sweater or blanket, shipped to a store, bought by a customer, washed many times at home, and eventually thrown away or donated. Every single one of those steps uses energy and causes some environmental impact — but none of them appear in this diagram, because they are all outside the fence.
This study’s boundary stops the moment the finished yarn leaves the mill. That is a common choice called cradle to gate — it covers everything from the sheep farm (the “cradle”) up to the exit of the last factory (the “gate”), and nothing after.
Here is the what-if question: what if the boundary had also included the energy used to transport the yarn to a garment factory, and then the garment factory itself — the cutting, sewing, and finishing of a finished sweater? Do you think the total carbon footprint number would go up, go down, or stay the same — and why?
Student: it would go up clearly
AI: Exactly right — and that is the single most important thing to understand about system boundaries.
Every time you widen the fence to include more steps, the number goes up — because you are counting more real activity that causes real emissions. A narrow boundary will always produce a smaller number than a wide one, even if they are studying the same product.
This matters enormously in a business context. When a wool supplier hands you an LCA result showing a low carbon footprint, the system boundary is the first thing to check — not the number. Two suppliers can report very different footprints for the same material simply because one drew a wider fence than the other. Neither number is necessarily wrong, but they are not the same thing, and you cannot compare them directly.
The system boundary is one decision inside a bigger set called goal and scope — the opening chapter of every LCA study, where researchers decide why the study is being done, who it is for, and exactly where the fence gets drawn. Would you like to explore how system boundary fits into that bigger goal-and-scope picture, or is there anything about the boundary concept you’d like to dig into first?
Student: So do people argue over the system boundary
AI: This is a perfectly normal question — and yes, absolutely they do!
System boundary disagreements are actually one of the most common arguments in sustainability reporting. A wool producer might publish a cradle-to-gate number that stops at the mill gate, while an environmental group might argue that the study should have gone all the way to end-of-life disposal. Both are using real data — but because the fences are drawn in different places, they get very different numbers, and each side can accuse the other of cherry-picking.
This is also where greenwashing can happen — not necessarily through lying, but through choosing a conveniently narrow boundary and not being upfront about it. A brand might advertise “our wool sweater has a footprint of only 2 kg CO₂” — but if that number only covers the final spinning mill and nothing else, it leaves out the sheep farm, which in our wool yarn example is responsible for roughly 86% of the total impact.
So the practical skill for someone in fashion buying or brand management is not to memorise carbon numbers — it is to always ask: “What is inside the fence, and what did you leave out?”
Would you like to explore the full goal and scope concept next, which is where all these boundary decisions get formally written down at the start of a study?
Student: stop the skill

title: /system-boundary cotton_fiber
text:
/system-boundary cotton_fiber
Skill version: 0.1 Student: diana Model: gpt-5-5 Date: 2026-06-18
AI: Imagine you are reviewing a restaurant receipt at the end of a work dinner.
The receipt only shows the food and drinks your table ordered. It does not include the taxi you took to get there, the parking fee your colleague paid, or the round of drinks someone bought at the bar next door.
Here’s the question: if someone added up only the restaurant receipt to figure out the total cost of the evening, would that number be accurate, and what would be missing from it?
Student: not accurate
AI: Exactly. The restaurant receipt only covers what happened inside that restaurant. Everything else, even if it was real and costly, simply does not appear on it.
In Life Cycle Assessment, or LCA (a way of measuring environmental impact across a product’s life), every study has a “receipt” too. That boundary is called the system boundary. Think of it as a fence around part of the supply chain.
Everything inside the fence is measured and counted. Everything outside the fence is ignored.
For this cotton fiber study, the fence includes: - Fertilizer production - Cotton farming
Looking at that boundary, what cotton-related steps might happen after cotton farming that are not being counted here?
Student: do you have graph to show me
AI: Yes. Here is the cotton fiber supply chain diagram:
 ../../skills_references/cotton_fiber/product_graph_structure.svg
Each box is one step that this study does count.
For this cotton fiber case, the study counts: - Fertilizer production - Cotton farming
The fence, or system boundary, goes around those two boxes together.
Anything after cotton farming, such as spinning cotton into yarn, weaving fabric, sewing garments, shipping to stores, customer washing, or disposal, is outside the fence and not counted here.
Student: what else is impotant about system boundary
AI: The most important thing is that the system boundary controls what the final number means.
If the boundary is narrow, the result will usually look smaller. If the boundary is wider, the result will usually look larger because more steps are being counted.
For cotton fiber, this study counts: - Making synthetic fertilizer - Growing and ginning the cotton fiber
It does not count: - Spinning cotton into yarn - Weaving or knitting fabric - Dyeing - Sewing a garment - Shipping to stores - Customer washing and drying - Disposal or recycling
That matters because two companies could both say “our cotton has a low footprint,” but they might not be measuring the same thing. One company might only count the farm. Another might count farm, fertilizer, textile processing, transport, and disposal.
So the first question a buyer, brand manager, or sustainability team should ask is:
“What is inside the boundary, and what is outside it?”
That question protects you from comparing two numbers that look similar but are actually measuring different parts of the product’s life.

title: /life-cycle-stages wool_yarn
text:
/life-cycle-stages wool_yarn
Skill version: 0.1 Student: elena Model: sonnet-4-6 Date: 2026-06-14

AI: Here is a quick question before we look at any LCA numbers.
Imagine two friends both track their spending for a month. One tracks everything — rent, food, transport, nights out, the lot. The other only tracks their grocery bills. At the end of the month, who spent less?
The one who only tracked groceries — obviously. But is that a fair comparison?
Student: no it’s not fair
AI: Exactly — they were measuring different things. One covered the full picture, the other covered only a slice of it. The grocery number is not wrong, but you cannot compare it to the full-spending number and draw any conclusion about who is better at managing money.
In LCA, the same problem comes up constantly. Researchers have agreed on four standard ways to draw the fence — four named boundary types that describe where a study starts and where it stops. These are called life cycle stages (meaning: the named phases of a product’s life that a study can choose to include or exclude).
Knowing which stage a study covers is the first thing to check before you trust any footprint number — because the same product will get a completely different result depending on which stages are inside the fence.
Let’s go through all four using wool yarn as our example. Here is the first one:
Cradle to gate — this boundary starts at the very beginning of the supply chain, where the raw material comes from (the “cradle”) and stops at the factory exit (the “gate”). For wool yarn, that means the study covers the sheep farm and the yarn production mill — and nothing else. What happens to the yarn after it leaves the mill is outside the fence.
Before I go on — why do you think most supplier sustainability reports use cradle to gate rather than a wider boundary?
Student: because they can only control what happens on their side
AI: Exactly right — and that is a really important insight.
A wool yarn supplier controls the sheep farm and the mill. They have no control over what a fashion brand does with the yarn after they buy it — whether they knit it into a jumper, how that jumper gets washed, or where it ends up at the end of its life. It would not be fair to hold them responsible for impacts they cannot influence.
Now the other three boundary types, quickly:
Cradle to grave — starts at the same place as cradle to gate (the sheep farm) but continues all the way through to the very end of the product’s life. For a wool jumper made from this yarn, that would add the garment factory, the customer wearing and washing it for years, and eventually donating or disposing of it. This gives the most complete picture but requires estimates about consumer behaviour that can be hard to get right.
Cradle to cradle — the same as cradle to grave, but instead of ending at a bin, the end-of-life material loops back into production as recycled input. For wool, this could mean old garments being collected, shredded, and re-spun into new yarn — completing the circle.
Gate to grave — the opposite of cradle to gate. It starts at the warehouse or retail store and covers only what happens after purchase: the customer using the product and eventually disposing of it. All the production upstream is left out.
Here is the wool yarn supply chain diagram:
 ../../skills_references/wool_yarn/product_graph_structure.svg
The two boxes shown — sheep farming and yarn production — are everything this study included. Based on the four boundary types we just covered, which one does this diagram represent?
Student: cradle to gate
AI: Correct — and you can see exactly why just by looking at the diagram. The study starts at the sheep farm (the cradle) and ends when the finished yarn leaves the mill (the gate). Nothing after that point appears in the diagram, which means nothing after that point was counted.
Here is the what-if question: if a garment brand bought this wool yarn and wanted to do a cradle-to-grave study of the finished jumper — including the customer wearing it, hand-washing it, and eventually donating it to a charity shop — what extra steps would they need to add inside the fence that are not shown in that diagram?
Student: the garment factory, washing at home, and disposing of it
AI: Perfect — that is exactly the three things that would need to be added, and in the right order too.
This is the key insight the whole skill has been building toward: the same wool yarn has a different footprint number depending on which boundary you use. The cradle-to-gate number only reflects the farm and the mill. The cradle-to-grave number adds the garment factory, decades of home washing, and end-of-life disposal — and for a wool jumper that gets washed regularly over many years, that additional impact is not small.
This is why, when a supplier hands you a footprint number, the first question to ask is not “is that number high or low?” — it is “which boundary does that number cover?” A cradle-to-gate number and a cradle-to-grave number for the same product are not comparable, even if they are sitting side by side on the same page.
Would you like to move on to goal and scope — the full set of opening decisions every LCA study makes, of which boundary type is just one part? Or is there anything about the four boundary types you would like to look at more closely?

Student: Diana
Model used: GPT-5.5 Fast
Tested arguments: cotton_fiber, polyester_tshirt, wool_yarn
The following report preserves the polished English summary created from the Korean learning and testing process.



This session tested how clearly the LCA teaching skill can explain three fashion-related life cycle assessment case studies to a beginner.
LCA means Life Cycle Assessment. It is a way to study the environmental impacts of a product across the stages of its life, from raw material production through manufacturing, use, and disposal.
The session focused on three arguments:

cotton_fiber
polyester_tshirt
wool_yarn

The main testing questions were:

What does each argument mean in this LCA project?
What functional unit should be used?
What system boundary should be used?
What life cycle stages are included?
Which stages are likely to create the largest environmental impacts?
What data would be needed to calculate impacts properly?
What does the current reference material explain well?
What is missing from the current reference material?
What future LCA skill should be created next?






cotton_fiber represents the production of cotton fiber.
It does not represent a finished cotton T-shirt or finished garment. It focuses on the early material stage, where cotton is grown and prepared as fiber for later textile production.
In simple terms, this case is about the environmental impact of producing the cotton fiber that could later become yarn, fabric, and clothing.



The appropriate functional unit is:
1 kg of ginned cotton fiber, ready for spinning
A functional unit is the exact thing being measured. It works like a price-per-unit label in retail. Without a consistent unit, comparisons can be misleading.
This functional unit is appropriate because cotton_fiber is about fiber, not yarn, fabric, or a finished garment.



The current reference material uses a simplified cradle-to-gate boundary:
Synthetic nitrogen fertilizer production → cotton farming
In a fuller real-world cotton fiber LCA, the boundary could also include:

Seed production
Cotton cultivation
Harvesting
Transport to the ginning facility
Ginning
Fiber packaging
Pesticide and herbicide production
Land use change

The current model is intentionally simplified for teaching.



A broader cotton fiber life cycle can include:

Input preparation
Cotton cultivation
Harvesting
Transport to ginning
Ginning
Fiber preparation and packaging

The current reference material mainly includes:

Fertilizer production
Cotton farming




The main environmental issues for cotton_fiber are:

Nitrogen fertilizer use
Nitrous oxide emissions from fertilized soil
Water use
Carbon dioxide from farm energy and fertilizer production

The current reference result shows:
Global warming: 5.97 kg CO2 eq per 1 kg cotton fiber
The reference material also includes:
Water use: 8,000 L per 1 kg cotton fiber
CO2 eq means carbon dioxide equivalent. It converts different greenhouse gases into one common climate impact unit.



The skill explains these points well:

Cotton fiber is an early material stage, not a finished garment.
The functional unit is 1 kg of cotton fiber.
Nitrogen fertilizer is important.
Natural fibers can still have significant environmental impacts.
Nitrous oxide can strongly affect climate results.
Water use is an important cotton issue.




The current reference material does not fully cover:

Pesticide and herbicide production
Ginning as a separate process
Transport
Land use change
Seed production
Spinning
Fabric production
Garment manufacturing
Consumer use
End-of-life







polyester_tshirt represents the production of one polyester T-shirt.
Unlike cotton_fiber, this case is closer to a finished product. It follows a simplified supply chain from crude oil extraction to polyester fiber production and T-shirt assembly.
The key beginner-friendly message is:
A polyester T-shirt is connected to fossil fuel extraction because polyester is made from petroleum-based feedstock.



The appropriate functional unit is:
1 polyester T-shirt, ready for sale, approximately 200 g of fabric
This is appropriate because the case is about a garment item, not just a fiber or yarn material.



The current system boundary is:
Crude oil extraction → polyester fiber production → T-shirt assembly
This is a cradle-to-gate model. It does not include consumer use, washing, drying, disposal, recycling, or microfiber pollution.



A broader polyester T-shirt life cycle can include:

Crude oil or natural gas extraction
Chemical feedstock production
Polyester resin production
Polyester fiber production
Yarn production
Fabric production
Dyeing and finishing
Cutting and sewing
Packaging and distribution
Consumer use
End-of-life

The current reference material includes:

Oil extraction
Polyester fiber production
T-shirt assembly




The main environmental issues are:

Fossil fuel use
Crude oil extraction
Polyester fiber production energy
Carbon dioxide emissions
Methane leakage from oil extraction

The current reference result shows:
Global warming: 2.535 kg CO2 eq per polyester T-shirt
The model also shows that one T-shirt is linked to:
0.3 kg of crude oil extraction



The skill explains these points well:

Polyester is a fossil-fuel-based synthetic material.
A finished T-shirt can be traced back to crude oil extraction.
Compound scaling across supply chain steps matters.
Methane leakage from oil extraction can affect climate results.
Upstream raw material impacts can be assigned to a final garment.




The current reference material does not fully cover:

Dyeing and finishing
Transport between stages
Washing and drying during use
End-of-life
Microfiber or microplastic pollution
Recycled polyester comparison
Product weight variation beyond the 200 g assumption







wool_yarn represents the production of wool yarn.
It does not represent a finished sweater or garment. It focuses on sheep farming and wool yarn production.
In simple terms, this case is about turning wool from sheep into yarn that can later be used for knitting or weaving.



The appropriate functional unit is:
1 kg of wool yarn, ready for knitting or weaving
This is appropriate because the case focuses on yarn as an intermediate textile material.



The current system boundary is:
Sheep farming → wool yarn production
This includes the farm and the yarn production facility.



A broader wool yarn life cycle can include:

Sheep farming
Shearing
Raw wool storage
Transport
Scouring
Carding or combing
Spinning
Dyeing
Packaging

The current reference material includes:

Sheep farming
Wool yarn production




The main environmental issues are:

Methane emissions from sheep
Carbon dioxide from farm and processing energy
Raw wool loss during processing
Water use in yarn production

The current reference result shows:
Global warming: 13.55 kg CO2 eq per 1 kg wool yarn
The current material also shows:
Water use: 30 L per 1 kg wool yarn
The model requires:
1.1 kg raw wool to produce 1 kg wool yarn



The skill explains these points well:

Wool yarn is an intermediate material, not a finished garment.
The functional unit is 1 kg of wool yarn.
Sheep farming is a major upstream stage.
Methane is a major climate issue.
Natural fibers are not automatically low-carbon.
Raw wool losses during yarn production affect the final result.




The current reference material does not fully cover:

Sheep feed production as a separate upstream process
Land use change
Transport between farm and mill
Scouring wastewater treatment
Dyeing
Animal welfare
Garment manufacturing
Consumer use
End-of-life







The three arguments use different functional units:



Argument
Functional Unit




cotton_fiber
1 kg cotton fiber


polyester_tshirt
1 polyester T-shirt, approximately 200 g


wool_yarn
1 kg wool yarn



This means the results should not be compared directly as a simple ranking.
The polyester result is for one 200 g T-shirt, while the cotton and wool results are per 1 kg of material.






Argument
Global Warming Result




cotton_fiber
5.97 kg CO2 eq / kg cotton fiber


polyester_tshirt
2.535 kg CO2 eq / T-shirt


wool_yarn
13.55 kg CO2 eq / kg wool yarn



These numbers are useful for teaching, but they are not directly comparable unless the functional units and system boundaries are aligned.










Argument
Main Hotspot




cotton_fiber
Nitrogen fertilizer and water use


polyester_tshirt
Fossil fuel feedstock and polyester fiber production


wool_yarn
Sheep farming and methane emissions






All three cases follow a broad fashion supply chain pattern:
Raw material source → material processing → textile or product production
However, the raw material source is different in each case:

cotton_fiber starts with a plant crop.
polyester_tshirt starts with crude oil.
wool_yarn starts with sheep.




The three arguments show that different material types create environmental impacts in different ways.

Cotton is plant-based, but fertilizer and water use matter.
Polyester is synthetic and fossil-fuel-based.
Wool is animal-based, and methane from sheep can dominate climate impact.





The skill currently does well at:

Explaining each argument in beginner-friendly language
Defining functional units clearly
Explaining simplified supply chains
Identifying the main environmental hotspot in each case
Connecting LCA results to fashion and retail decisions
Warning students that “natural” does not automatically mean “low impact”
Explaining that missing stages affect the interpretation of results




The current skill is limited because the reference materials are simplified teaching examples.
The main limitations are:

Different functional units across the three arguments
Different system boundaries
Missing use phase data
Missing end-of-life data
Missing transport data
Missing dyeing and finishing data
Limited water and land use detail
Limited chemical and wastewater detail
No animal welfare data for wool
No microfiber pollution data for polyester




The next recommended skill is:
Fair LCA Comparison Skill
Suggested command name:
/fair-comparison
The purpose of this skill would be to teach students how to compare LCA results fairly.
It should focus on:

Functional units
System boundaries
Product weight
Use phase assumptions
End-of-life assumptions
Why LCA numbers cannot be compared without checking the basis of comparison

The key teaching question should be:
Are we comparing the same thing?



The three arguments provide a strong beginner-friendly foundation for learning LCA.
cotton_fiber teaches that plant-based fibers can have major impacts from fertilizer and water use.
polyester_tshirt teaches that synthetic garments are connected to fossil fuel extraction and manufacturing energy.
wool_yarn teaches that animal-based fibers can have large climate impacts from methane emissions.
The most important next step is to teach students how to compare these cases fairly by checking the functional unit and system boundary before interpreting the results.



This testing process helped clarify several important LCA lessons.

I learned that the same word, such as “cotton,” “polyester,” or “wool,” can refer to very different points in a supply chain.
I learned that cotton_fiber is a material-stage case, not a finished clothing case.
I learned that polyester_tshirt is closer to a finished product case because it uses one T-shirt as the functional unit.
I learned that wool_yarn is an intermediate material case because it focuses on yarn before it becomes a sweater, fabric, or garment.
I learned that the functional unit is one of the most important parts of an LCA because it defines what the result actually means.
I learned that comparing LCA results is unfair if the functional units are different.
I learned that system boundaries matter because a result changes depending on whether it includes only production, or also use, washing, drying, disposal, and recycling.
I learned that natural fibers are not automatically low impact.
I learned that cotton can have important impacts from water use, nitrogen fertilizer, and nitrous oxide.
I learned that polyester can have important impacts from fossil fuel extraction, polyester fiber production, and manufacturing energy.
I learned that wool can have important impacts from sheep farming and methane emissions.
I learned that missing stages, such as dyeing, transport, wastewater treatment, use phase, or end-of-life, must be clearly explained so readers do not overinterpret the numbers.
I learned that LCA results are not just numbers; they are business decision tools for material sourcing, supplier questions, product claims, and sustainability communication.

The most important overall lesson was:
Before comparing LCA results, check whether the studies are measuring the same thing and including the same life cycle stages.



The next LCA skill session should improve in the following ways.

It should explicitly teach students how to compare functional units fairly.
It should warn students when one result is per kilogram and another result is per product unit.
It should include a simple conversion exercise, such as comparing a 200 g polyester T-shirt with 1 kg material results.
It should include a system boundary checklist so students can see which stages are included and which are missing.
It should explain that a zero result in an impact category may mean “not modeled,” not “no environmental impact.”

cotton_fiber represents the production of cotton fiber.
It does not represent a finished cotton T-shirt or finished garment. It focuses on the early material stage, where cotton is grown and prepared as fiber for later textile production.
In simple terms, this case is about the environmental impact of producing the cotton fiber that could later become yarn, fabric, and clothing.



The appropriate functional unit is:
1 kg of ginned cotton fiber, ready for spinning
A functional unit is the exact thing being measured. It works like a price-per-unit label in retail. Without a consistent unit, comparisons can be misleading.
This functional unit is appropriate because cotton_fiber is about fiber, not yarn, fabric, or a finished garment.



The current reference material uses a simplified cradle-to-gate boundary:
Synthetic nitrogen fertilizer production → cotton farming
In a fuller real-world cotton fiber LCA, the boundary could also include:

Seed production
Cotton cultivation
Harvesting
Transport to the ginning facility
Ginning
Fiber packaging
Pesticide and herbicide production
Land use change

The current model is intentionally simplified for teaching.



A broader cotton fiber life cycle can include:

Input preparation
Cotton cultivation
Harvesting
Transport to ginning
Ginning
Fiber preparation and packaging

The current reference material mainly includes:

Fertilizer production
Cotton farming

Carbon dioxide from farm energy and fertilizer production

The reference material also includes:

CO2 eq means carbon dioxide equivalent. It converts different greenhouse gases into one common climate impact unit.

Cotton fiber is an early material stage, not a finished garment.
The functional unit is 1 kg of cotton fiber.
Nitrogen fertilizer is important.
Natural fibers can still have significant environmental impacts.

Ready to hear about the two big questions every LCA has to answer before a single number gets calculated?
Student: yes
AI: Every LCA study has to answer two questions right at the start. Together they are called the goal and scope — and they are written down before any numbers are calculated, so that anyone reading the results later knows exactly what they are looking at.
The goal is the “why” and the “who.” In LCA, the goal is a short statement that says why the study is being done and who it is for — it matters because the same product can have a very different study design depending on whether the results are for an internal decision, a public label, or a legal certification. For this cotton study, the goal is: to calculate the climate and eutrophication impact of producing 1 kg of cotton fiber, so that buyers can understand what the supply chain actually contributes to environmental damage. The audience is a fashion brand sourcing team — people like you — comparing supplier claims.
The scope is the “what is in and what is out.” Think of it like a fence drawn around the supply chain — everything inside the fence is studied, everything outside is ignored. For this study, the fence encloses two steps: P1 — Fertilizer production and P2 — Cotton farming. The study stops the moment the cotton fiber leaves the farm gate, ready for spinning. What happens after that — transport, spinning, weaving, garment manufacturing — is outside the fence. This type of scope has a name: cradle to gate, meaning from the raw material in the ground all the way to the factory exit, but no further.
Does that distinction between goal and scope make sense so far — or would it help to have an example of what a different goal might look like for the same product?
Student: go ahead
AI: Here is something worth thinking about — a small change to the scope that would have a big effect on the result.
This study leaves out pesticides and herbicides — the chemicals sprayed on cotton fields to kill insects and weeds. Producing those chemicals takes energy and releases CO₂, just like the fertilizer factory does. The researchers made a deliberate choice to exclude them in order to keep the study simple and focused on nitrogen chemistry.
What if a competing cotton supplier ran their LCA and also left out pesticides — but their farming system actually uses more pesticide than yours? Their footprint number would look similar to yours on paper, even though their real-world impact is higher.
Do you think that kind of gap — where two studies use the same scope label (“cradle to gate”) but quietly exclude different things — could make supplier comparisons misleading?
Student: yes
AI: Exactly right — and this is one of the most important things to understand about sustainability data in fashion sourcing.
Two suppliers can both hand you a “cradle to gate” LCA and show similar numbers, while one has quietly excluded pesticides, transport, or seed production, and the other has included them. The label sounds the same but the fence is drawn in a different place. Without checking what is actually inside the fence, you cannot compare the two numbers fairly at all.
This is why, as a buyer or merchandiser, the first question to ask when a supplier shares an LCA result is not “what is the number?” — it is “what is inside the system boundary?” Sustainability certifications like the Higg Index or the European Environmental Footprint exist partly to solve this problem by forcing all suppliers to draw the fence in the same place, so comparisons are actually fair.
A number without a clearly stated scope is not evidence — it is just a number.

That wraps up the five steps for cotton fiber! Would you like to see how goal and scope decisions play out in a different context — for example, a footwear study or a retail logistics scenario?
Student: can you give me some examples other than this one?
AI: Absolutely! Here are two examples from very different parts of the retail world.

Example 1 — Footwear
A trainer brand runs an LCA on a running shoe. Their goal is to reduce the product’s footprint for an upcoming sustainability campaign aimed at consumers. Because the audience is the public — not a sourcing team — they need to include the full life of the shoe, not just manufacturing.
So their scope is cradle to grave: raw materials, factory, transport to store, the customer wearing and washing the shoes over two years, and finally disposal or recycling. If they had stopped at the factory gate (cradle to gate), the study would have missed the fact that the rubber sole releases microplastics during use — which turns out to be a significant part of the story.

Example 2 — E-commerce packaging
An online retailer wants to cut packaging waste. Their goal is to compare a cardboard box to a reusable fabric mailer — not to reduce production emissions, but to reduce what ends up in landfill. Because the question is about what happens after the customer receives the parcel, the scope they choose is gate to grave: it starts at the warehouse and ends when the packaging is thrown away or returned. The factory that made the cardboard is outside the fence — irrelevant to the decision they are trying to make.

Both examples show the same principle: the goal drives the scope. Change the question you are trying to answer, and the fence moves.
Would you like to explore another example, or does this feel like a good place to wrap up?
Student: save it as a session with a version

title: /functional-unit wool_yarn
text:
/functional-unit wool_yarn
Skill version: 0.2 Student: elena Model: sonnet-4-6 Date: 2026-06-13

AI: Before we look at any numbers — imagine a wool supplier sends you a data sheet claiming their yarn has a “low carbon footprint.” What unit would you want the number to be measured in — per kilogram of yarn, per sweater it could knit, or per year of wearing the sweater?
Student: per kilogram of yarn
AI: That is actually a really strong instinct — and as it turns out, it is exactly what the researchers chose for this study. Well done.
Here’s why it works so well: when you are comparing two suppliers of raw material (say, a New Zealand wool farm versus an Australian one), measuring per kilogram gives you a fair, apples-to-apples comparison. Neither supplier is penalised for the fact that one sweater design might use more or less yarn than another — you are just measuring the material itself, at the point it leaves the mill.
The study we will be working through is called Wool Yarn — 1 kg. It traces the carbon footprint of producing 1 kg of wool yarn, following the journey from the sheep farm all the way through to the spinning mill. It is a teaching example built for this course, so the numbers are illustrative rather than from a specific brand — but they are calibrated to be realistic.
Here is what the supply chain looks like:
 ../../skills_references/wool_yarn/product_graph_structure.svg
You can see two boxes connected by an arrow. The rightmost box — P2 — Wool yarn production — has a special name in LCA: it is called the reference process. That just means it is the finishing line — the step that delivers the finished product. Everything to its left exists only to supply it. The functional unit is precisely what comes out of that box: 1 kg of wool yarn, ready for knitting or weaving.
Ready to hear what that 1 kg of yarn actually costs the planet in CO₂?
Student: yes
AI: In LCA, the precise definition of exactly what we are measuring is called the functional unit — it exists so that comparisons between products are fair and no one can fudge the numbers by measuring something slightly different.
For this study, the functional unit is: 1 kg of wool yarn, ready for knitting or weaving.
That one phrase does a lot of work. It tells you the quantity (1 kg), the product (wool yarn), and the condition it must be in (ready to use). A supplier who delivers tangled raw fleece doesn’t count — it has to be finished yarn.
As for the carbon cost: producing that 1 kg releases roughly 14.9 kg of CO₂ equivalent. To put that in perspective, that is about the same as driving a car for 120 kilometres. And here is the surprising part — about 86% of that footprint comes not from the factory, but from the sheep farm. The methane that sheep release during digestion (yes, from belching) is a very potent greenhouse gas, and it adds up fast.
One unit that would give a misleading answer here would be per sweater — because sweater sizes vary wildly, and a chunky-knit jumper uses three times as much yarn as a fine-knit one, making fair comparisons almost impossible.
What if a competing wool supplier measured their footprint per sweater produced instead of per kilogram — could that make their yarn look better or worse than yours, even if the underlying process was identical?
Student: it could make their yarn look better
AI: Exactly right — and that is a really important insight.
If a competitor’s yarn is used mainly in lightweight, fine-knit designs that only need 200g per sweater, then measuring “per sweater” makes their footprint look tiny — even if the yarn itself is produced in exactly the same way as yours. Meanwhile, your yarn might go into heavy winter knitwear using 600g per sweater, so your “per sweater” number looks three times worse — through no fault of your production process at all.
This is why unit choice is never neutral. A supplier, a brand, or even a certification body can make a product look more or less sustainable just by choosing a different measuring stick — without changing a single thing about how it is made.
So as a buyer or merchandiser, the very first question to ask when a supplier hands you a sustainability certificate is: “Per what unit?” A carbon number without a clear unit attached to it is not a claim you can act on — it is just a number.

That wraps up the five steps for wool yarn! Would you like to see how the functional unit works in a different area — for example, footwear, home textiles, or retail logistics?
Student: yes, show me footwear. Is this a new example?
AI: Great question — and good instinct to ask! No, it is not a full new case study like the wool yarn one we just worked through. Think of it more like a bonus example from a reference guide. The wool yarn lesson had its own dedicated file with real numbers to calculate; this is a shorter illustration designed to show how the same concept applies in a completely different corner of the fashion industry.
When researchers do an LCA on a pair of shoes, a very common functional unit is:
1 pair of shoes, worn for 3 years.
Notice how different this feels from the yarn example. Instead of just measuring a material at the factory gate, this unit includes time. Why? Because with footwear, how long the product lasts matters enormously for whether it is actually sustainable.
Imagine two trainers: - Brand A: costs £40, footprint of 8 kg CO₂, falls apart after 6 months - Brand B: costs £120, footprint of 14 kg CO₂, lasts 3 years
Measured per pair produced, Brand A looks much better. But measured per pair worn for 3 years, you would need to buy Brand A six times over — meaning 48 kg CO₂ total — compared to Brand B’s 14 kg CO₂.
The unit “1 pair worn for 3 years” stops a cheap, short-lived product from hiding behind a low production number.
Would you like to explore another area — home textiles or retail logistics — or does this feel like a good place to wrap up for today?

title: /functional-unit cotton_fiber
text:
/functional-unit cotton_fiber
Skill version: 0.1 Student: calvin Model: sonnet-4-6 Date: 2026-06-13

AI: Before we look at any numbers — imagine you’re a sourcing manager at a fashion brand, and two cotton suppliers both send you a data sheet claiming their cotton has a lower carbon footprint. What is the very first question you would ask before you could even start comparing those two numbers?
Student: what unit was used
AI: Exactly right — that is the single most important question, and experienced sustainability professionals ask it every time.
If one supplier measured their footprint per kilogram of cotton and the other measured it per bale (a bale is roughly 220 kg), the numbers are completely incomparable — even if the underlying environmental impact is identical. You’d be looking at 5.6 vs 1,232 and thinking one is catastrophically worse, when really they’re the same.
That instinct — per what? — is the entire concept we’re about to explore.
The study we’ll be working through is called Cotton Fiber — 1 kg. The goal is to calculate the climate impact of producing cotton fiber, tracing the supply chain all the way back from the cotton field to the fertilizer factory that supplies it. It’s a teaching example built for this course, so the numbers are illustrative rather than from a specific brand — but they’re calibrated to be realistic for irrigated cotton systems.
Here’s the shape of the supply chain:
 ../../skills_references/cotton_fiber/product_graph_structure.svg
You can see two boxes connected by an arrow. The rightmost box — P2 — Cotton farming — has a special name in LCA: it’s called the reference process. That just means it’s the finishing line — the step that delivers the finished product. Everything to its left exists only to supply it. The fertilizer factory (P1) is there for one reason only: to feed the cotton farm.
The functional unit is precisely what comes out of that reference process box.
What do you think comes out of P2? What is the cotton farm actually delivering?
Student: the fiber
AI: Exactly — the fiber. That’s the finished product this entire supply chain exists to produce.
So here is the functional unit for this study, stated precisely:

1 kg of ginned cotton fiber, ready for spinning

In LCA, this is called the functional unit — it is the precise definition of exactly what is being measured, so that comparisons between products are fair.
Notice how specific it is. Not just “cotton” — but ginned cotton (meaning the seeds have already been removed), and ready for spinning (meaning it’s in the form a textile mill would actually receive and use). That level of precision matters: if one supplier measures at the farm gate before ginning, and another measures after, you’re still not comparing the same thing.
Why 1 kg specifically? Because at the raw material stage, buyers and suppliers deal in weight. A sourcing manager comparing two fiber suppliers will ask: for every kilogram I buy, what is the environmental cost? It’s a natural, neutral unit for material-level comparisons — before the fiber becomes yarn, fabric, or a finished garment.
What it rules out: measuring per bale, per field, or per growing season — all of which would make comparisons between farms of different sizes completely meaningless.
Suppose a competing cotton supplier claims their fiber has a footprint of only 2.1 kg CO₂ — lower than the 5.6 kg CO₂ in this study. But when you read the fine print, you discover they measured per kg of raw seed cotton, before ginning — and it takes roughly 3 kg of seed cotton to produce 1 kg of ginned fiber. Would their number still look better once you account for that?

title: /damage-characterization polyester_tshirt
text:
/damage-characterization polyester_tshirt
Skill version: 0.1 Student: elena Model: sonnet-4-6 Date: 2026-06-16
AI: Let’s get started. Before any LCA terms, here’s a question to set up the big idea.
Imagine you run an online store and you’re watching two numbers this week: website visits, and actual revenue. Visits went up 20%. Does that tell you, by itself, how much more money you made?
What else would you need to know — about your conversion rate, your average order value, maybe even what day of the week it is — before “visits” actually translates into “dollars”?
Student: No, visits going up 20% tells you almost nothing about revenue on its own.
AI: Exactly — visits alone tell you almost nothing about revenue. You’d need the conversion rate, the average order value, maybe seasonality — extra assumptions that connect the “easy to count” number to the “actual outcome” number.
The midpoint impact scores you’ve already calculated — kg CO₂-eq, kg SO₂-eq, PM 2.5-eq — are a bit like “website visits.” They are useful, standardized, and based on solid chemistry. But they are not yet the actual real-world outcome anyone ultimately cares about: how many people got sick, how much of an ecosystem was damaged, how much harder it will be to get raw materials in the future.
Damage characterization is the step that takes midpoint scores the rest of the way — translating “kg CO₂-eq” into estimated harm across three areas of protection: human health, ecosystem quality, and resource availability. It requires more assumptions than the midpoint step, the same way “visits to dollars” requires more assumptions than just counting visits — so damage scores carry more uncertainty than midpoint scores. But for some audiences, that tradeoff is worth it, because “X years of healthy life lost” communicates real stakes in a way “X kg of CO₂-eq” does not.
Let’s look at the midpoint scores you already calculated for Polyester T-shirt, and reason about where each one’s damage actually lands.
The polyester T-shirt scored on two midpoint categories: Global warming and Smog formation. Which damage area does ground-level smog primarily harm, given that it’s mostly known as an air-quality problem people breathe in? And does Global warming stop at human health, or does it also reach ecosystems?
Student: Smog harms human health; warming reaches ecosystems too
AI: Exactly right on both counts. Smog formation is almost entirely a human-health story — ground-level ozone is a respiratory irritant that’s breathed in directly. And Global warming is one of the few midpoints that reaches more than one damage area at once: it raises heat-related illness and disease spread (human health), while also shifting habitats and stressing species (ecosystem quality).
Here’s the what-if: a brand wants to tell investors their product “protects biodiversity.” Which of this product’s two midpoint scores is actually relevant to that claim, and which one is not?
Student: Global warming, since it reaches ecosystem quality
AI: Exactly — Global warming is the relevant one, since it’s the only score here that reaches ecosystem quality at all. Smog formation, no matter how the brand frames it, doesn’t actually speak to biodiversity — it’s purely a human-health number. If a brand leaned on their smog score to support a “protects biodiversity” claim, that would be a mismatch between the evidence and the claim.
Here’s a practical takeaway for product development:

Knowing which damage area a midpoint score feeds into helps you target improvements to what your specific audience cares about. A community worried about local air quality cares about particulate matter and smog — human health categories. An investor focused on biodiversity pledges cares about acidification and eutrophication — ecosystem categories. The same supply chain change can matter enormously to one audience and barely register with another.

You’ve now followed an emission all the way from a raw inventory number, through a midpoint impact score, to the real-world damage area it lands in. The next natural question for a business is: out of this whole supply chain, which single process is actually responsible for the lion’s share of any of these scores? That is what hotspot analysis answers — and it’s the skill that turns all of this maths into a one-sentence recommendation a business can act on.
Would you like to explore that next, or is there anything about damage areas you’d like to dig into further first?

/impact-characterization polyester_tshirt
Skill version: 0.1 Student: elena Model: sonnet-4-6 Date: 2026-06-16
AI: The argument you typed was “polyester tshirt” — I’ll treat that as polyester_tshirt, one of the three case studies set up for this lesson (the others are wool_yarn and cotton_fiber).
Let’s get started with an everyday analogy before touching any LCA terms.
Imagine a moving company’s rate card. Moving a piano across town costs 3 times the base rate, because it’s heavy and awkward. Moving that same piano overseas costs 10 times the base rate, because of customs and crating. Moving a couch across town costs 1 times the base rate. Moving that same couch overseas costs 4 times the base rate.
Here’s the question: does the piano have one single “multiplier,” or does it have a different multiplier depending on which kind of move you’re asking about? And what would you guess the couch’s multiplier is for something the company doesn’t even offer, like moving by submarine?
Student: Each move has a different multiplier, and the submarine would be zero
AI: Exactly — the piano isn’t “worth 3” or “worth 10,” it’s worth different amounts depending on which kind of cost you’re calculating. And you’ve got the submarine right too: if the company doesn’t offer that kind of move, the sensible number for that combination is zero, not a guess.
Characterization factors in LCA work exactly like that rate card. They are not one number attached to a substance — they form a whole table. The rows are substances (CO₂, methane, ammonia…). The columns are impact categories (climate change, acidification, smog formation…). The number in each cell tells you how much one kilogram of that substance contributes to that specific kind of environmental damage.
Ammonia, for example, has a real number in the acidification column, a different real number in the particulate matter column, and a flat zero in the climate change column — because ammonia does not trap heat the way CO₂ does. Zero is a real, deliberate answer in this table, not a missing one.
