AI: Imagine you manage a clothing label. Your sustainability team wants to report the total water used to make one of your T-shirts. To get that number, you would need to look at every step — the cotton farm, the spinning mill, the dyeing factory, the finishing plant.
Each step has its own water usage figure. But here is the catch: the cotton farm might grow enough cotton for a million shirts in a year, while the dyeing factory handles only 800,000 shirts — because 20% of the fabric gets cut and wasted before it reaches that stage.
So here is the question: if you wanted to know the total water used for just one shirt, could you simply add up each factory’s yearly water usage and divide by a million? Or would that give you the wrong answer — and if so, why?

Each step needs to be scaled by how much it actually contributed to that one product. That careful scaled total is what LCA calls the life cycle inventory.
Think of it like a receipt from nature. Instead of money, it lists kilograms of CO₂ and litres of water. And instead of showing what each factory spent separately, it shows the combined total — the sum of everything that crossed from the human-made world into the natural world to make exactly one unit of the finished product.

title: /system-boundary cotton_fiber
text:
/system-boundary cotton_fiber
Skill version: 0.1 Student: calvin Model: sonnet-4-6 Date: 2026-06-14

AI: Imagine you are reviewing a restaurant receipt at the end of a work dinner. The receipt only shows the food and drinks your table ordered — it does not include the taxi you took to get there, the parking fee your colleague paid, or the round of drinks someone bought at the bar next door.
Here’s the question: if someone added up only the restaurant receipt to figure out the total cost of the evening, would that number be accurate — and what would be missing from it?
Student: no it would not
AI: You’ve got it — and that gap between the receipt and the full picture is the central tension in LCA too.
In Life Cycle Assessment, every study has a “receipt” — a defined set of steps it covers and a defined set it does not. That boundary is called the system boundary. Think of it as a fence drawn around part of the supply chain. Everything inside the fence is measured and counted. Everything outside the fence is ignored — even if it causes real environmental harm.
The system boundary is not a flaw — it is a deliberate choice. But it means the number you get at the end of a study only tells you about what was inside the fence.
Let’s look at a real example — a study of Cotton Fiber. The goal is to calculate the environmental impact of producing 1 kg of ginned cotton fiber, tracing the supply chain from the fertilizer factory through to the cotton farm.
Here is the supply chain diagram:
 ../../skills_references/cotton_fiber/product_graph_structure.svg
Each box in this diagram is a step the study decided to include. The fence — the system boundary — runs around both of these boxes together. Any step that does not appear is outside the fence and was not counted.
Looking at the diagram, can you spot any steps you might expect to be there that are not shown? For example — think about what the cotton farm needs to operate beyond fertilizer. What else goes into growing cotton that might have its own environmental footprint?
Student: harvesting, pesticides
AI: Exactly right — and those are two really important ones.
Pesticides and herbicides have to be manufactured in a chemical factory before they ever arrive at the farm — and that manufacturing process uses energy and releases emissions. But in this study, the production of pesticides is completely outside the fence. The study includes the fertilizer factory but stops there — the pesticide factory is not shown in the diagram and was not counted at all.
Harvesting is similar — the diesel fuel burned by the harvesting machinery does appear indirectly (it is folded into the CO₂ figure for the cotton farm), but the manufacturing of the harvesting machine itself was left out.
Here is the what-if question: if the study had also included the production of all the pesticides and herbicides used on the farm — which had to be manufactured somewhere before they arrived — do you think the total carbon footprint would look bigger or smaller than the number this study reports?
Student: bigger
AI: Exactly — every time you pull something from outside the fence and bring it inside, the number goes up.
And this matters in a very practical way for anyone working in fashion or retail. Cotton has a reputation as a “natural” fiber — grown in a field, not made in a chemical plant. But this study already shows that just the fertilizer factory alone adds significantly to the footprint. If you also counted the pesticide factories, the seed production, the transport to the spinning mill, and eventually the disposal of the finished garment, the number would keep climbing with every step you added.
When a cotton supplier hands you an LCA result, the system boundary is the first thing to check — not the number. Two suppliers can report very different footprints for the same cotton simply because one drew a wider fence than the other. You can only compare them fairly if they used the same boundary — otherwise you are comparing two different receipts and assuming they cover the same meal.
The system boundary is one decision inside a bigger set called goal and scope — the opening chapter of every LCA study, where researchers decide why the study is being done, who it is for, and exactly where the fence gets drawn. Would you like to explore how boundary decisions fit into that bigger goal-and-scope picture, or is there anything about the boundary concept you’d like to dig into first?
Student: can people fudge the system boundary
AI: This is a really good question — and the honest answer is yes, it happens.
It is not always outright lying. The most common version is simply choosing a conveniently narrow boundary and either not mentioning it clearly, or burying it in the fine print. A cotton supplier might publish a footprint number that only covers the farm itself — leaving out the fertilizer factory entirely — because that makes the number look smaller. Nothing in the report is technically false, but the reader walks away with an incomplete picture.
This is one of the main mechanisms behind greenwashing — making a product look more sustainable than it really is, not by inventing data, but by carefully choosing where the fence goes. In our cotton example, the fertilizer factory alone contributes about 0.7 kg of CO₂ equivalent per kg of cotton. Leave that out, and the footprint suddenly looks much more flattering.
The defence against this — both as a buyer and as a brand manager — is always to ask the same two questions when you see an LCA number: “What is inside the fence?” and “What did you leave out, and why?” A trustworthy study will answer both questions clearly and upfront.
Would you like to explore the full goal and scope concept next, where these boundary decisions get formally written down — or is there anything else about system boundary you’d like to dig into?

AI: Here is a question to start us off — no LCA knowledge needed yet.
Imagine you are reviewing a restaurant receipt at the end of a work dinner. The receipt shows the food and drinks your table ordered — but it does not include the taxi you took to get there, the parking fee your colleague paid, or the round of drinks someone bought at the bar next door.
If someone added up only the restaurant receipt to figure out the total cost of the evening, would that number be accurate — and what would be missing from it?
Student: it would be missing the taxi and parking costs
AI: Exactly right — the receipt only covers what happened inside that restaurant. The taxi, the parking, the drinks next door — all of those were real costs that actually happened that evening, but because they were outside the restaurant’s bill, they simply do not appear. The total on the receipt is not wrong, but it is incomplete.
Life Cycle Assessment works the same way. Every study has its own version of that receipt — a defined set of steps it covers and a defined set it does not. That defined edge is called the system boundary (meaning: the line that separates what is counted from what is not). Everything inside the boundary is measured and added up. Everything outside is ignored, even if it causes real environmental harm.
Now let’s look at a real example. This study is called the Polyester T-shirt. Its goal is to calculate the climate impact of producing one T-shirt, tracing the journey from crude oil in the ground all the way to a finished garment ready for sale.
Here is the supply chain diagram — each box is a step that this study decided to include:
 ../../skills_references/polyester_tshirt/product_graph_structure.svg
The fence — the system boundary — runs around all three of those boxes together. Any step not shown in the diagram is outside the fence and was not counted.
Looking at the diagram, can you think of anything that happens to the T-shirt after it leaves the last box that might also cause environmental impact — but is not shown here?
Student: washing and drying it
AI: Exactly right — and that is a really important observation.
Every time a customer washes and tumble-dries a polyester T-shirt, that machine is using electricity and heating water, which releases CO₂. Over the lifetime of a T-shirt — which might be washed 50 or 100 times — that adds up to a significant amount of environmental impact. But none of that is captured in this study, because the boundary stops the moment the shirt leaves the factory.
This study is what’s called cradle to gate — meaning it starts at the very beginning of the supply chain (the oil well, which is the “cradle”) and stops at the factory exit (the “gate”). Everything that happens after the gate — the shop, the customer’s wardrobe, the washing machine, the bin — is outside the fence.
Here is the what-if question: if this study had included all those washes and tumble-dry cycles over the T-shirt’s lifetime, do you think the total carbon footprint would go up a little, or a lot — and why?

title: /technosphere-and-ecosphere polyester_tshirt
text:
/technosphere-and-ecosphere polyester_tshirt
Skill version: 0.1 Student: elena Model: sonnet-4-6 Date: 2026-06-15

AI: Imagine a busy town that has a wall around it. Inside the wall: houses, factories, shops, roads — everything built and run by people. Outside the wall: fields, rivers, the sky, the forest — nature, exactly as it would be without humans.
Now imagine a factory inside the wall burns coal to run its machines. Two things happen: first, a truck drives through the town and delivers the coal (that coal never leaves the wall — it moves from one part of the human world to another). Second, the chimney sends smoke up into the sky above the wall — and that smoke drifts out beyond the wall into the fields and the river.
Here is the question: which of those two things — the coal truck or the chimney smoke — actually crosses the wall and reaches the natural world outside?
Student: chimeny
AI: Exactly right — the chimney smoke is the one that crosses the wall. The coal truck stayed inside the town the whole time, moving from one human-made place to another without ever touching the natural world. The smoke drifting out over the fields and into the river — that is where environmental harm begins.
In Life Cycle Assessment, researchers use two names for these two worlds. The human-made world — everything inside the wall, like factories, farms, mills, and trucks — is called the technosphere (from “techno”, meaning made by people). The natural world outside the wall — air, water, soil, living ecosystems — is called the ecosphere (from “eco”, meaning the living environment).
The key idea is this: environmental harm only happens when something crosses the boundary between the two. Emissions released into the ecosphere (like CO₂ into the air) are the flows that cause impact. Everything that moves around inside the technosphere stays inside the wall and does not directly harm the natural world.
Now let’s sort a real LCA study into these two worlds. This is the product graph for Polyester T-shirt — 1 unit.
 ../../skills_references/polyester_tshirt/product_graph_structure.svg
Inside the wall — the technosphere: The three boxes in this diagram are the processes — the human activities that make the T-shirt. In this study that means Oil extraction, Polyester fiber production, and T-shirt assembly. Also inside the wall are the intermediate products flowing between those boxes: crude oil moving from the well to the fiber plant, and polyester fiber moving from the fiber plant to the garment factory. Those flows stay entirely inside the human-made world — they never touch nature.
Crossing the wall — into the ecosphere: Two substances are emitted from this supply chain into the natural world: - Carbon dioxide — released to air at all three stages: the oil well, the fiber plant, and the garment factory. - Methane — released to air at the oil well only, as a fugitive leak (meaning it escapes from pipelines and equipment, rather than being burned deliberately).
In LCA, these crossings are called elementary flows — the basic exchanges between the human world and the natural world. They are the only flows that score as environmental impact, because they are the only ones that actually reach the ecosphere.
Carbon dioxide appears at all three stages of this supply chain, but methane only appears at the oil well. Which one do you think causes more total climate harm in this study — carbon dioxide or methane?
Student: carbon dioxide
AI: You are absolutely right this time — and it is worth noticing that this is the opposite of the wool yarn result. In the wool yarn study, methane dominated because sheep produce so much of it during digestion. Here, carbon dioxide is the bigger culprit because it is released at every single stage: the oil well, the fiber plant, and the garment factory. Adding those up gives about 2.16 kg of CO₂ crossing into the ecosphere, compared to only 0.42 kg CO₂ equivalent from the methane leaking at the oil well.
This is an important reminder that the technosphere-ecosphere framework is not a one-size-fits-all answer — you have to look at the specific crossings in each study to know where the real impact is hiding.
Now here is the what-if question for this study. The carbon dioxide in this supply chain comes almost entirely from burning fossil fuels to run machines — at the oil well, at the fiber plant, and at the garment factory. The technosphere flows (the crude oil, the polyester fiber, the T-shirt itself) stay inside the wall.
Imagine the garment factory switched to solar panels instead of coal-fired electricity. Which part of the LCA would change — the technosphere processes, the ecosphere crossings, or both?
Student: the ecosphere crossings
AI: That is exactly right — and it is a really sharp answer. The technosphere processes would stay the same: oil still gets extracted, fiber still gets made, the T-shirt still gets assembled. What would change is the crossing — the CO₂ that currently leaves the factory chimney and enters the ecosphere. Solar panels generate electricity without burning anything, which means nothing crosses the wall from that factory. The garment assembly stage would go from 1.0 kg of CO₂ into the air down to nearly zero.
This is a powerful insight for anyone working in fashion procurement. A brand that moves its garment factories to renewable energy is not changing its technosphere supply chain — the same countries, the same factories, the same materials. But it is reducing its ecosphere crossings, which means it is genuinely reducing environmental impact, not just rearranging steps inside the wall.
Here is the sharper version of that question to keep in your toolkit: when a supplier claims their product is “greener” or “more sustainable”, ask — did they reduce their ecosphere crossings, or did they just change something inside the technosphere? Switching from one oil-based dye to another, repackaging in recycled boxes, moving production to a different country — none of those necessarily reduce what crosses the wall. Only fewer emissions to air, fewer resources drawn from nature, and fewer substances discharged to water represent genuine improvement.
The technosphere-ecosphere boundary is the reason LCA studies track elementary flows — that is the official name for the crossings we have been talking about. The natural next step is understanding how those crossings get converted into impact scores — a process called characterisation, which is where the CO₂ and methane numbers get turned into a single comparable figure. Would you like to explore that, or is there anything about the two worlds you would like to revisit?

title: /what-is-impact-assessment cotton_fiber
text:
/what-is-impact-assessment cotton_fiber
Skill version: 0.1 Student: elena Model: sonnet-4-6 Date: 2026-06-16
AI: Let’s get started. Before any LCA terms, here’s a question to set up the big idea.
Imagine you run a retail chain with stores in the US, the UK, and Japan. At the end of the month, your US stores report $40,000 in sales, your UK stores report £25,000, and your Japan stores report ¥3,000,000.
Here’s the question: can you find your total global sales just by adding 40,000 + 25,000 + 3,000,000? Why or why not — and what would you need to do first before those three numbers could be added together?
Student: You’d need to convert each currency to a common one first
AI: Exactly — you’d use the day’s exchange rate to convert pounds and yen into dollars, and only then could you add the three numbers together into one meaningful total.
Life cycle assessment has exactly this problem. The inventory you’ve already learned about lists emissions in their own original units — kg of CO₂, kg of nitrous oxide, kg of ammonia, litres of water. You cannot add a kilogram of nitrous oxide to a kilogram of CO₂ any more than you can add pounds to yen — they cause different kinds of environmental damage at different intensities.
The step that solves this is called life cycle impact assessment, or LCIA. It uses conversion numbers — called characterization factors — that work just like exchange rates. Each factor tells you how much damage one kilogram of a substance causes, relative to a reference substance, for a specific type of damage. For climate change, the reference substance is CO₂, so every other greenhouse gas gets converted into “kg of CO₂ equivalent.” Once everything is in the same unit, you can finally add it up into one score.
Let’s convert the inventory for Cotton Fiber into impact scores together.

Here’s the what-if: a cotton brand is told their fertilizer use is the source of nearly all the acidification and particulate matter scores — not the climate score, which is dominated by CO₂ and N₂O instead. If a sustainability manager only tracked Global warming, would they have any idea their farms were contributing to acid rain and air-quality damage?
Student: so can you explain to me about this skill easily?
AI: Of course — totally normal to want a quick recap. Here’s the whole idea in the simplest way I can put it:
The problem: When you make something (like cotton fiber), the farm and factory release several different things into the air and water — carbon dioxide, nitrous oxide, ammonia, and so on. Each one is measured in its own units, like kilograms. But you can’t just add “1.5 kg of CO₂” and “0.015 kg of nitrous oxide” together and call it one number — that’s like adding dollars and yen without converting first. They’re different “currencies” of pollution.
The fix: Impact assessment is the step that converts each pollutant into a common scale, the same way an exchange rate converts yen into dollars. Scientists have already figured out, for each substance, “how much worse is this than the reference substance, kilogram for kilogram?” That conversion number is called a characterization factor. Once everything is converted into the same unit (like “kg of CO₂ equivalent”), you can finally add them up into one meaningful score.
The result: Instead of one giant combined number for “all pollution,” you get a short list of separate scores — one for climate change, one for acid rain, one for air quality, and so on — because those are genuinely different kinds of harm that shouldn’t be mixed together.
That’s really the whole skill in one paragraph. Does that land more clearly? If so, want to go ahead and take a stab at the what-if question above, or would you like me to re-explain any one part of it first?
Student: so this is a skill that unify all the different units in one to calculate the impact correct?
AI: You’re very close — just one small but important correction.
It does unify units, but not into one single unit for everything. It converts the raw units into a common unit within each type of damage — so all the greenhouse gases (CO₂, nitrous oxide, methane) get converted into “kg CO₂ equivalent” for the climate change score. But the substances that cause acid rain get converted into a different common unit — “kg SO₂ equivalent” — for the acidification score. And particulate matter pollution gets converted into yet another unit, “PM 2.5 equivalent.”
So you end up with several small, unified totals — one per type of damage — not one giant unified number for “total impact.” That’s deliberate: climate change and acid rain and air quality are genuinely different kinds of harm, and squashing them into a single number would hide which one actually matters for a given business decision.
Does that distinction make sense — many small “common currencies,” one per category, rather than one currency for everything?
Student: make it to one sentence to understand.
AI: Impact assessment converts each pollutant’s raw amount into a common unit within its own type of damage — using a conversion number called a characterization factor — so you get one meaningful score per damage type (climate, acid rain, air quality, etc.), not one giant combined score for everything.

Here is a question fashion buyers face all the time: a cotton T-shirt and a polyester T-shirt are sitting on a desk in front of you. A colleague says the cotton one is more sustainable because it is natural. Another colleague says the polyester one is more sustainable because it lasts longer.
Who is right — and how would you actually find out?
Student: we have to actual mearuse some stuff
AI: That is exactly the right instinct — and it gets to the heart of why LCA exists. A gut feeling or a label on a hanger cannot settle that question. You have to actually measure what goes into making each shirt, trace every step, and add up the results.
That is what Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) is: a method for adding up all the environmental impacts of making a product by tracing every step in its supply chain. Think of it like a receipt that shows every hidden cost — not money, but things like CO₂ emissions, water use, and chemical pollution.
Ready to walk through how a study like that is structured?
Student: yes
AI: Here is why this matters for someone working in fashion or retail.
When a supplier sends you a sustainability certificate, LCA is the method behind it. Without LCA, “sustainable” is just a word on a hangtag — with it, you can ask: sustainable compared to what, measured how, and over which part of the product’s life?
LCA also tells you where the biggest environmental impacts actually are. Maybe 80% of a shirt’s carbon footprint comes from the fabric mill, not the cotton farm — that changes where a designer or buyer should focus their efforts.

Here is the map of how an LCA study works — four phases. Think of it like a recipe with four steps:

Goal and scope — Decide why you are doing the study and draw a fence around what you are including. Without this step, the results cannot be compared fairly to anything else.
Inventory — Collect the data. How much cotton? How much electricity? How much water? A big spreadsheet for every step inside the fence.
Impact assessment — Convert the raw data into environmental scores. Turn kilograms of CO₂ and methane into a single climate-change number, so you can see the big picture.
Interpretation — Read the results and decide what to do. Where is the impact coming from? What can you change?

Which of those four phases do you think would be the hardest to do in practice — and why?
Student: 3
AI: Good pick — and you are not alone in that. Phase 3 trips a lot of people up at first.
Here is why it feels hard: the inventory gives you a big list of different emissions — CO₂, methane, ammonia, sulfur dioxide — all measured in kilograms. But you cannot just add them up, because a kilogram of methane warms the planet about 28 times more than a kilogram of CO₂. It is like adding up amounts in different currencies — euros, yen, pounds — without knowing the exchange rates.
Impact assessment is the currency exchange. It uses published conversion numbers (called characterization factors) to translate every emission into a common unit — like “kg of CO₂ equivalent” — so you can add them together and see the total climate impact.
That is the concept. In the next skill (impact characterization), you actually do the maths by hand with real data. But first — every LCA study has to start with the first phase: goal and scope, deciding why you are doing the study and what you include. Would you like to explore that one next, or ask something else about LCA first?

You have just identified something that trips up a lot of sustainability marketing: a claim like “this fabric is eco-friendly” is meaningless unless you say compared to what, measured how, and over how long.
This is precisely the problem that LCA — Life Cycle Assessment was invented to solve. LCA is a method for adding up all the environmental impacts of making, using, and disposing of a product by tracing every step in its supply chain. Think of it like a receipt that shows every hidden cost of a product — not in money, but in CO₂ emissions, water use, and chemical pollution. It forces you to be specific about exactly what you are measuring and over what period of time, so that comparisons are actually fair.
For someone working in fashion sourcing or buying, this matters in a very practical way: when a supplier hands you a sustainability certificate, LCA is the method behind it. AI: Of course! Here are a few more situations where “it depends” is exactly the right answer — and where LCA is the tool that helps you find out what it depends on.

A tote bag vs a plastic bag
A cotton tote bag takes a lot of energy and water to produce — far more than a single plastic bag. Studies have shown you need to use a cotton tote around 150 times before its carbon footprint per use drops below a disposable plastic bag’s. So is the tote more sustainable? It depends entirely on how many times you actually use it.

Organic cotton vs conventional cotton
Organic cotton avoids synthetic pesticides, which sounds like a clear win. But organic farming typically produces less cotton per acre, which means more land is needed to grow the same amount of fibre. More land can mean more water use and more habitat disruption. Is organic better? It depends on which environmental problem you care most about — chemical pollution, water, or land use.

A wool jumper vs a polyester fleece
Wool is natural and biodegradable. But sheep release methane during digestion, and methane is a very potent greenhouse gas — far more warming than CO₂ kilogram for kilogram. A polyester fleece has no methane problem, but it is made from fossil fuels and sheds microplastics when washed. Which is worse? It depends on whether you are more concerned about climate change, fossil fuel use, or ocean pollution.

In every case, LCA is the tool that replaces “it depends” with an actual number — so you can make the comparison honestly.

title: Plan: Adding the BAFU-2025-LCI Database and openLCA LCIA Methods Pack
text:
This plan describes two separate additions to the project that work well together:

The BAFU-2025-LCI database — a free Swiss background process database that provides life cycle inventory data for hundreds of materials, fuels, and transport modes. Think of it as a reference library of emission numbers for common industrial processes — so instead of hand-entering “nylon 6 emits ~9 kg CO₂ per kg produced”, you just connect to the BAFU nylon process and the software looks it up automatically.
The openLCA LCIA methods pack — a free file that adds new impact assessment methods to the openLCA server. The most useful additions are:

EF 3.1 — the European Commission’s Environmental Footprint method (16 impact categories)
ReCiPe 2016 Midpoint (H) — the most widely used global LCA method (18 impact categories)
CML, ILCD, and several others


These two additions are independent — you can import one without the other. But together they let you: (a) stop entering CO₂ numbers by hand for common materials, and (b) score the results using European and global impact methods rather than just the US-focused TRACI 2.2.






BAFU stands for Bundesamt für Umwelt — the Swiss Federal Office for the Environment. BAFU:2025 is the Swiss Federal Administration’s official life cycle inventory database, released in 2025 and made freely available under Switzerland’s Open Government Data strategy.
The database contains 11,747 life cycle inventories across 176 categories, covering construction, mobility, energy, metals, chemicals, paper, agriculture, food, consumption, and waste management. It is one of the largest freely available LCA databases in the world.

Download: https://nexus.openlca.org/database/BAFU
More info: https://esu-services.ch/bafu2025/
Case study (plastic broom): https://www.openlca.org/case-study-lca-of-a-plastic-broom-using-bafu2025/

More categories = more complete picture — TRACI’s 9 categories miss water consumption and land use entirely. For a cotton garment, those two categories are huge. EF 3.1 and ReCiPe capture them.
European vs American standards — a company selling in the EU may be required to report using EF methodology. Understanding what that means, and why it differs from TRACI, is genuine industry knowledge.
The hotspot can shift — a product that looks “clean” on climate change may score poorly on land use or water consumption. Seeing all 16 categories at once prevents greenwashing by cherry-picking the best metric.




The plastic broom from the video is an excellent introductory example because: - It has only two materials (nylon bristles + PLA handle) - It has only one process (broom production) - The hotspot is clear and surprising (PLA, not nylon) - The transport scenario shows that transport often matters less than materials - 1.70 vs 1.78 kg CO₂ eq teaches that short transport routes alone won’t solve the problem if the material itself is high-impact

title: Plan: Adding the BAFU-2025-LCI Database and openLCA LCIA Methods Pack
text:
This plan describes two separate additions to the project that work well together:

The BAFU-2025-LCI database — a free Swiss background process database that provides life cycle inventory data for hundreds of materials, fuels, and transport modes. Think of it as a reference library of emission numbers for common industrial processes — so instead of hand-entering “nylon 6 emits ~9 kg CO₂ per kg produced”, you just connect to the BAFU nylon process and the software looks it up automatically.
The openLCA LCIA methods pack — a free file that adds new impact assessment methods to the openLCA server. The most useful additions are:

EF 3.1 — the European Commission’s Environmental Footprint method (16 impact categories)
ReCiPe 2016 Midpoint (H) — the most widely used global LCA method (18 impact categories)
CML, ILCD, and several others


These two additions are independent — you can import one without the other. But together they let you: (a) stop entering CO₂ numbers by hand for common materials, and (b) score the results using European and global impact methods rather than just the US-focused TRACI 2.2.

title: PLAN: Life Cycle Assessment MCP
text:
A fully open-source, freely deployable MCP (Model Context Protocol) server that exposes life cycle assessment as AI-callable tools — the same way the Dolt MCP exposes a version-controlled SQL database to any AI assistant.
Once deployed, any AI — Claude.ai, ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini — can run a full LCA in a single conversation turn, get back numbers and supply chain diagrams, and explain the results to a student in plain English. No software to install. No files to open. No code to write.




The Dolt MCP gives AI assistants a small set of focused tools for talking to a database:



Dolt MCP Tool
What it does




list_tables
See what data is available in the database


describe_table
Understand the shape of a specific table


list_views
See pre-built views (named queries)


read_query
Ask a question using SQL — get rows back


write_query
Insert or update rows



A student can open Claude.ai, ask “What are the top 5 products by revenue this quarter?” and Claude calls read_query behind the scenes, gets the rows, and answers in plain English. The student never writes SQL.
The Life Cycle Assessment MCP does the same thing for environmental analysis.












LCA MCP Tool
Dolt analogy
What it does




list_impact_methods
list_tables
See all 45 scoring methods available (TRACI 2.2, ReCiPe 2016, EF 3.1 …)


check_server
connect / ping
Confirm the calculation engine is running


run_lca
read_query
Pass a supply chain description, get back full results + diagrams


get_lca_svg
describe_table
Get a visual supply chain map without running the full calculation









A student in a retail sustainability course asks Claude.ai:

“Which is better for the environment — a paper cup or a polystyrene foam cup? I want to see the actual numbers.”

Claude calls run_lca twice — once for each cup — passing the supply chain descriptions (product graphs) on behalf of the student. It gets back:



Impact
Paper cup
PS foam cup




Global warming
0.011 kg CO₂ eq
0.005 kg CO₂ eq


Freshwater withdrawn
14.3 L
0.7 L



And two supply chain diagrams like this one — generated automatically and returned as SVG images Claude can display inline:



Paper cup supply chain


Claude then explains: “The PS foam cup produces about half the greenhouse gas emissions of the paper cup — but it relies on non-renewable petroleum and doesn’t biodegrade. The paper cup uses 20× more water because pulping and papermaking are extremely water-intensive. Which trade-off matters more depends on what your company is trying to prioritise.”
The student never saw the product graph. They just asked a question.




A student comparing textile materials asks:

“I’m sourcing yarn for a new product line. Is wool or cotton better for climate impact?”

Claude calls run_lca for each, gets back TRACI 2.2 results, and can show:
Wool yarn (1 kg): - Global warming: 13.55 kg CO₂ eq — dominated by methane from sheep - Water: 30 L
Cotton fiber (1 kg): - Global warming: 1.50 kg CO₂ eq - Water: 8,000 L — cotton farming is one of the most water-intensive crops
Claude explains: “Wool has nearly 9× the climate impact of cotton — because sheep emit large amounts of methane, a greenhouse gas 25× more potent than CO₂. But cotton requires thousands of litres of water per kilogram. If your brand is in a water-stressed region, cotton may be the harder choice despite its lower carbon number.”
Supply chain diagrams are returned for both and shown side by side.




A student asks: “What if the wool farm switched to renewable electricity for processing?”
Claude edits the product graph in memory, calls run_lca again with the updated values, and compares the before and after — all in one conversation turn. No files to open. No re-running scripts.




A student asks: “What scoring methods are available? Can we look at this using ReCiPe instead of TRACI?”
Claude calls list_impact_methods, shows the student the 45 available methods, and re-runs the same analysis with ReCiPe 2016 — again, all in the same conversation.





When a student asks a sustainability question, the AI:

Looks up the relevant product graph (or writes one from the student’s description)
Calls run_lca(product_graph="...", method="TRACI 2.2")
Receives LCI totals, LCIA scores, a scaling vector, and two SVG diagrams
Displays the diagrams inline and explains the numbers in plain English

The student sees only the explanation and the diagrams. The product graph, the tool call, and the raw JSON never appear.







Layer
Technology




MCP framework
fastmcp (Python)


HTTP/SSE transport
FastAPI + uvicorn

title: PLAN: Life Cycle Assessment MCP
text:
A fully open-source, freely deployable MCP (Model Context Protocol) server that exposes life cycle assessment as AI-callable tools — the same way the Dolt MCP exposes a version-controlled SQL database to any AI assistant.
Once deployed, any AI — Claude.ai, ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini — can run a full LCA in a single conversation turn, get back numbers and supply chain diagrams, and explain the results to a student in plain English. No software to install. No files to open. No code to write.

title: PLAN: Life Cycle Assessment MCP
text:
A student in a retail sustainability course asks Claude.ai:

“Which is better for the environment — a paper cup or a polystyrene foam cup? I want to see the actual numbers.”

Claude calls run_lca twice — once for each cup — passing the supply chain descriptions (product graphs) on behalf of the student. It gets back:



Impact
Paper cup
PS foam cup




Global warming
0.011 kg CO₂ eq
0.005 kg CO₂ eq


Freshwater withdrawn
14.3 L
0.7 L



And two supply chain diagrams like this one — generated automatically and returned as SVG images Claude can display inline:



Paper cup supply chain


Claude then explains: “The PS foam cup produces about half the greenhouse gas emissions of the paper cup — but it relies on non-renewable petroleum and doesn’t biodegrade. The paper cup uses 20× more water because pulping and papermaking are extremely water-intensive. Which trade-off matters more depends on what your company is trying to prioritise.”
The student never saw the product graph. They just asked a question.




A student comparing textile materials asks:

“I’m sourcing yarn for a new product line. Is wool or cotton better for climate impact?”

Claude calls run_lca for each, gets back TRACI 2.2 results, and can show:
Wool yarn (1 kg): - Global warming: 13.55 kg CO₂ eq — dominated by methane from sheep - Water: 30 L
Cotton fiber (1 kg): - Global warming: 1.50 kg CO₂ eq - Water: 8,000 L — cotton farming is one of the most water-intensive crops
Claude explains: “Wool has nearly 9× the climate impact of cotton — because sheep emit large amounts of methane, a greenhouse gas 25× more potent than CO₂. But cotton requires thousands of litres of water per kilogram. If your brand is in a water-stressed region, cotton may be the harder choice despite its lower carbon number.”
Supply chain diagrams are returned for both and shown side by side.




A student asks: “What if the wool farm switched to renewable electricity for processing?”
Claude edits the product graph in memory, calls run_lca again with the updated values, and compares the before and after — all in one conversation turn. No files to open. No re-running scripts.




A student asks: “What scoring methods are available? Can we look at this using ReCiPe instead of TRACI?”
Claude calls list_impact_methods, shows the student the 45 available methods, and re-runs the same analysis with ReCiPe 2016 — again, all in the same conversation.

title: Plan: Production LCIA with ReCiPe 2016 as an Alternative to TRACI 2.2
text:
ReCiPe 2016 is a widely used life cycle impact assessment method developed jointly by RIVM (Netherlands National Institute for Public Health), Radboud University, and PRé Consultants. The name is a play on the word “recipe” because it combines several earlier European methods (CML, Eco-indicator 99) into one.
ReCiPe is the most common LCIA method used in European and global LCA studies. TRACI 2.2 (the method currently used in this project) is the US EPA’s method and is calibrated for North American conditions. For fashion and textile studies that span global supply chains — farms in India, mills in China, factories in Bangladesh — ReCiPe is often a better fit because its characterization factors are derived from global rather than US-only models.







Feature
TRACI 2.2
ReCiPe 2016




Origin

Geographic scope

Global

Yes (3 damage areas)

Yes (European + global)

Yes (built in)
No — not included


Available via LCIA methods pack?
Yes
Yes (free download)


Available in ecoinvent?
Yes
Yes (built in)





ReCiPe operates at two levels that work together:
Midpoint (problem-oriented) — 18 categories, similar in concept to TRACI’s categories. Each midpoint score is in its own unit and measures a specific type of environmental stress (e.g. global warming in kg CO₂ eq, freshwater use in m³, land use in m² per year).
Endpoint (damage-oriented) — 3 aggregated scores that translate midpoint impacts into damage to three “areas of protection”: - Human Health (DALY — disability-adjusted life years) - Ecosystems (species·year — local species loss over time) - Resource Scarcity (USD2013 — extra cost of future resource extraction)
For teaching, midpoints are easier to explain — each one corresponds to a recognisable environmental problem. Endpoints are more powerful for decision-making because they reduce 18 numbers to 3, but the aggregation involves value judgements that are harder to teach at introductory level.



ReCiPe comes in three versions reflecting different assumptions about time horizon and risk:









Perspective
Abbreviation
Time horizon
Use when




Individualist
(I)
Short (20 yr)
Optimistic / near-term


Hierarchist
(H)
Medium (100 yr)
Scientific consensus — recommended default


Egalitarian
(E)
Long (500 yr)
Precautionary / worst-case



Use ReCiPe 2016 Midpoint (H) as the default. The “(H)” stands for Hierarchist — it uses 100-year time horizons consistent with IPCC GWP100 and is the most commonly cited perspective in published LCA studies.

The cleanest path is to import the openLCA LCIA methods pack on top of the lca_methods database that is already running. This is a small free file (methods only, no background processes) that adds ReCiPe 2016, CML, EF, ILCD, and about a dozen other methods alongside TRACI 2.2.
Step 1 — Download the methods pack (one time only)

Go to https://nexus.openlca.org (free account required)
Search for “openLCA LCIA methods”
Download the latest .zip file (~few MB)
Place it anywhere accessible — e.g. $HOME/olca-data/

Step 2 — Import into the running database
Make sure the openLCA server is running (bash start_olca.sh), then import via the openLCA desktop app:

File → Import → Linked Data (JSON-LD) → select the .zip file → OK

Or try the API import endpoint:
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/import \
  -H "Content-Type: application/octet-stream" \
  --data-binary @"$HOME/olca-data/openLCA_LCIA_methods_2_2.zip"
Step 3 — Verify ReCiPe is now in the database
python3 -c "
from olca_ipc.rest import RestClient
import olca_schema as o
client = RestClient('http://localhost:8080')
for m in client.get_descriptors(o.ImpactMethod):
    print(m.name)
"
You should see ReCiPe 2016 Midpoint (H), (I), and (E) listed alongside TRACI 2.2. No restart needed.
Step 4 — Change one line in a product graph
# Before (TRACI):
lcia:
  method_name: "TRACI 2.2"

# After (ReCiPe):
lcia:
  method_name: "ReCiPe 2016 Midpoint (H)"
get_impact_method_ref() in lca_analysis.py does a case-insensitive substring search, so it will find the method automatically. No code changes needed. Run the analysis exactly as before.




Embed the CFs directly using the impact_categories block (same as the existing hand-typed CF path already in lca_analysis.py):
lcia:
  method: "ReCiPe 2016 Midpoint (H)"
  impact_categories:

    - name: Global Warming
      indicator: GWP100
      unit: kg CO2 eq
      characterization_factors:
        Carbon dioxide: 1.0
        Methane: 29.8
        Nitrous oxide: 273.0

    - name: Terrestrial Acidification
      indicator: TAP
      unit: kg SO2 eq
      characterization_factors:
        Sulfur dioxide: 1.0
        Nitrogen oxides: 0.56
        Ammonia: 2.45

    - name: Freshwater Eutrophication
      indicator: FEP
      unit: kg P eq
      characterization_factors:
        Phosphorus: 1.0

    - name: Fine Particle Formation
      indicator: PMFP
      unit: kg PM2.5 eq
      characterization_factors:
        Sulfur dioxide: 0.058
        Nitrogen oxides: 0.12
        Ammonia: 0.36

    - name: Water Consumption
      indicator: WCP
      unit: m3
      characterization_factors:
        Water: 0.001
This path requires no server and no database — pure Python multiplication using the existing impact_categories code path in lca_analysis.py.












Situation
Recommendation




lca_methods running, LCIA methods pack imported
Recommended — method_name: "ReCiPe 2016 Midpoint (H)"


No methods pack yet, want to test immediately
Fallback — embed CFs in product graph


ecoinvent connected
method_name: "ReCiPe 2016 Midpoint (H)" — built into ecoinvent


Comparing ReCiPe vs TRACI on same product
Change method_name and rerun — no other changes needed







Because method_name is just a string in the product graph, you can compare both methods by running the analysis twice with different values:
# Run with TRACI 2.2
python3 lca_scripts/lca_analysis.py lca_analysis/cotton_shirt/product_graph.yaml

# Edit product graph: change method_name to "ReCiPe 2016 Midpoint (H)"
# Run again
python3 lca_scripts/lca_analysis.py lca_analysis/cotton_shirt/product_graph.yaml
The GWP100 numbers should be very similar (both use IPCC AR6 GWP100 factors). Differences will appear in categories where the methods diverge — for example, TRACI uses North American spatial factors for acidification, while ReCiPe uses global average factors.




Comparing TRACI and ReCiPe results for the same product teaches students that:

The inventory (B·s) is fixed — the raw kg of CO₂, CH₄, etc. do not change. What changes is how those flows are weighted into impact scores.
The method is a value judgement — ReCiPe’s global factors vs TRACI’s North American factors reflects a choice about whose environment matters most in the assessment.
GWP is stable across methods — because both use IPCC GWP100. Students can trust the climate number regardless of which method is used.
Other categories diverge — acidification, eutrophication, and toxicity scores can differ significantly between TRACI and ReCiPe for the same product, especially for supply chains that span both US and non-US processes.






ReCiPe 2016 report: Huijbregts et al. (2017), ReCiPe 2016: A harmonized life cycle impact assessment method at midpoint and endpoint level. RIVM Report 2016-0104.
openLCA LCIA methods pack (free): https://nexus.openlca.org/database/openLCA%20LCIA%20methods
ReCiPe in openLCA: available via the methods pack or built into ecoinvent
FEDEFL flow mapping to ReCiPe: https://github.com/USEPA/fedelemflowlist (the same FEDEFL names work for both TRACI and ReCiPe lookups)

title: Plan: Production LCIA with ReCiPe 2016 as an Alternative to TRACI 2.2
text:
Because method_name is just a string in the product graph, you can compare both methods by running the analysis twice with different values:
# Run with TRACI 2.2
python3 lca_scripts/lca_analysis.py lca_analysis/cotton_shirt/product_graph.yaml

# Edit product graph: change method_name to "ReCiPe 2016 Midpoint (H)"
# Run again
python3 lca_scripts/lca_analysis.py lca_analysis/cotton_shirt/product_graph.yaml
The GWP100 numbers should be very similar (both use IPCC AR6 GWP100 factors). Differences will appear in categories where the methods diverge — for example, TRACI uses North American spatial factors for acidification, while ReCiPe uses global average factors.

title: Plan: Production LCIA with ReCiPe 2016 as an Alternative to TRACI 2.2
text:
Comparing TRACI and ReCiPe results for the same product teaches students that:

The inventory (B·s) is fixed — the raw kg of CO₂, CH₄, etc. do not change. What changes is how those flows are weighted into impact scores.
The method is a value judgement — ReCiPe’s global factors vs TRACI’s North American factors reflects a choice about whose environment matters most in the assessment.
GWP is stable across methods — because both use IPCC GWP100. Students can trust the climate number regardless of which method is used.
Other categories diverge — acidification, eutrophication, and toxicity scores can differ significantly between TRACI and ReCiPe for the same product, especially for supply chains that span both US and non-US processes.

title: Plan: Production LCIA with ReCiPe 2016 as an Alternative to TRACI 2.2
text:
ReCiPe 2016 report: Huijbregts et al. (2017), ReCiPe 2016: A harmonized life cycle impact assessment method at midpoint and endpoint level. RIVM Report 2016-0104.
openLCA LCIA methods pack (free): https://nexus.openlca.org/database/openLCA%20LCIA%20methods
ReCiPe in openLCA: available via the methods pack or built into ecoinvent
FEDEFL flow mapping to ReCiPe: https://github.com/USEPA/fedelemflowlist (the same FEDEFL names work for both TRACI and ReCiPe lookups)

title: Plan for Reference LCA Teaching Examples
text:
This document defines the format and content of the completed reference case studies used in this project. Each case study is a self-contained teaching package that provides enough information for an LLM-powered teaching skill to walk a student through any part of the LCA methodology using real numbers from that product.
The cases are designed for students at FIT (Fashion Institute of Technology) — business and retail management students with no programming background.




The reference teaching examples live in skills_references/ in the project root — separate from lca_analysis/, which holds examples tied to the openLCA server calculation workflow.
skills_references/
  wool_yarn/
  polyester_tshirt/
  cotton_fiber/
  ...
The teaching skills read from skills_references/<name>/ when given a case study argument. This keeps curated teaching material separate from ad-hoc analysis runs.




skills_references/<product>/
  product_graph.yaml              ← supply chain spec + LCIA method + characterization factors
  lca_results.md              ← pre-computed results: scaling vector, impacts by process and indicator
  product_graph_scaled.svg    ← supply chain diagram with scaling factors and flow amounts
  product_graph_structure.svg ← supply chain diagram with flow names only (no numbers)
  notes.md                    ← written teaching document: damage pathways, business narrative






The single quantitative source of truth for the case study. Contains two parts:
Part 1 — YAML frontmatter (the supply chain spec): - name — product name and functional unit description - goal — the study goal in plain language - functional_unit — what exactly is being measured (description, amount, unit) - units — unit definitions - products — all intermediate and final products in the supply chain - elementary_flows — emissions to air/water and resource extractions from nature - processes — each step in the supply chain with inputs, outputs, emissions, resources - reference_process — the process that delivers the functional unit - lcia — LCIA method name and impact categories with characterization factors (see below)
Part 2 — Markdown body (study notes): - Key assumptions table - Simplifications made - Source references - Any teaching notes specific to this product
The lcia: section format:
Simple (climate only):
lcia:
  method: IPCC AR6
  impact_categories:
    - name: Climate change
      indicator: GWP100
      unit: kg CO2 eq
      characterization_factors:
        CO2 to air: 1.0
        CH4 to air: 27.9
Multi-indicator:
lcia:
  method: EF 3.0
  impact_categories:
    - name: Climate change
      indicator: GWP100
      unit: kg CO2 eq
      characterization_factors:
        CO2 to air: 1.0
        CH4 to air: 27.9
        N2O to air: 273.0
    - name: Eutrophication (terrestrial)
      indicator: EP-terrestrial
      unit: mol N eq
      characterization_factors:
        NH3 to air: 3.54
        N2O to air: 0.27
The method name (e.g., “EF 3.0”, “IPCC AR6”) is the published standard the factors come from. The factors are embedded in the product graph so calculations work without requiring the LCIA method to be loaded in the openLCA database. The factors must match the named standard’s published values.




Pre-computed once (requires the openLCA server) and committed to the repository. Regenerate only when the product graph changes. Contains:

Goal and scope statement
Reference flow vector f
Technology matrix A
Scaling vector s = A⁻¹ · f (how much each process runs per functional unit)
Intervention matrix B (emissions per unit of each process)
LCI results B · s (total emissions per functional unit)
LCIA results (characterization factors applied — totals per impact category)
Contribution analysis (which process drives which impact, as a percentage)





Generated by lca_scripts/lca_svg.py from the product graph. Shows: - Each process as a labelled box - Scaling factor (s) on each box - Flow amounts on each arrow between processes - Emissions and resource flows as coloured side arrows




Generated by lca_scripts/lca_svg.py --structure from the product graph. Shows: - Each process as a labelled box - Flow names on arrows (no quantities) - Clean overview of supply chain structure




A written teaching document. Not generated — written by hand (or LLM-assisted). Contains:

LCIA method explanation — what EF 3.0 or IPCC AR6 is, why it was chosen for this product, what the indicators mean in plain language
Damage pathways — for each impact category, the full chain: emission → atmospheric/ecological mechanism → midpoint indicator → endpoint damage
Example for N2O:

N2O emitted from fertilised soil
Acts as a greenhouse gas (radiative forcing) AND depletes stratospheric ozone
Midpoint: GWP100 = 273 kg CO2 eq per kg N2O
Endpoint: climate change (human health, ecosystem quality) + UV exposure

Key findings — the main numbers, written for a business student: which process dominates, what surprised us, how the result compares to everyday reference points (km driven, days of electricity use, etc.)
Business relevance — what a sourcing, procurement, or product design decision could change based on this result






These three cases are designed as a teaching progression. Each adds exactly one new concept. All are directly relevant to fashion and textiles.



Folder: skills_references/wool_yarn/
Supply chain:
P1: Sheep farming  →  P2: Wool yarn production  [reference]
Depth: 1 layer. The sheep farm is one upstream node from the reference process. The scaling is straightforward: to produce 1 kg of yarn, you need 1.1 kg of raw fleece (10% waste in scouring and spinning), so the sheep farm runs at scale 1.1.
Emissions: - P1 (Sheep farming): CO2 (farm energy), CH4 (enteric fermentation — sheep digestion) - P2 (Wool yarn): CO2 (scouring, spinning energy)
LCIA method: IPCC AR6, GWP100 only
Key teaching moment: Sheep methane. CH4 has a GWP of 27.9 — nearly 28 times more potent than CO2. Wool’s “natural” reputation does not mean low-carbon.




Folder: skills_references/polyester_tshirt/
Supply chain:
P1: Oil extraction  →  P2: Polyester fiber production  →  P3: T-shirt assembly  [reference]
Depth: 2 layers. Oil extraction is two hops back from the finished T-shirt. Calculating the oil extraction’s contribution requires compound scaling: how much fiber per shirt × how much oil per kg of fiber.
Emissions: - P1 (Oil extraction): CO2 (combustion of energy), CH4 (fugitive from wells) - P2 (Polyester fiber): CO2 (polymerisation, energy; ~1.5 kg oil per kg fiber) - P3 (T-shirt assembly): CO2 (cutting, sewing, factory energy)
LCIA method: IPCC AR6, GWP100 only
Key teaching moment: “Your T-shirt is oil.” Polyester is a petroleum product. The matrix inversion shows how the emissions from the oil well end up attributed to the shirt, even though the well is two steps back in the supply chain.




Folder: skills_references/cotton_fiber/
Supply chain:
P1: Fertilizer production  →  P2: Cotton farming  [reference]
Depth: 1 layer. Same structural depth as wool yarn — but this case introduces a second impact category, making the LCIA step the main teaching focus.
Emissions: - P1 (Fertilizer): CO2 (energy-intensive production of synthetic nitrogen fertilizer) - P2 (Cotton farming): CO2 (machinery, irrigation energy), N2O (from fertilised soil — microbial conversion of nitrogen), NH3 (volatilisation from soil)
LCIA method: EF 3.0, two impact categories: - Climate change (GWP100): CO2, N2O, CH4 - Terrestrial eutrophication (EP-terrestrial): NH3, N2O
Key teaching moment: Cotton has a natural reputation but the field is the problem. N2O from the soil is 273× more potent than CO2 per kg. NH3 causes eutrophication — excess nitrogen in soil and waterways — independently of its climate contribution. The same emission (N2O) hits two different impact categories at once.

title: Plan: Adding LCIA Methods and Database Support to the run-lca Skill
text:
The current run-lca skill and lca_analysis.py script build a complete product system in openLCA and run a calculation. However the calculation only returns raw inventory results — e.g. “0.1 kg CO₂ per cup”. It does not produce impact scores (GWP in kg CO₂-eq, DALYs, species-years, etc.) because no LCIA method is passed to the CalculationSetup.
In other words, the skill currently stops at Step 2 (Characterisation) of the LCIA chain. Steps 3 and 4 (damage modelling, endpoint scores) are not reached.






The product graph format was designed from scratch to be readable for students. That was the right goal — but it was written without systematically checking every field against the olca-schema (the actual data format openLCA uses internally). Before extending the product graph with new fields, we need to confirm that every existing field maps cleanly onto a real olca-schema concept, and identify any gaps or mismatches.
The olca-schema example files live at: https://github.com/GreenDelta/olca-schema/tree/master/examples



Every object in openLCA is a JSON file with a @type field, a UUID @id, and typed fields. Here are the key types relevant to the product graph:
Process — one production step in the supply chain:
{
  "@type": "Process",
  "@id": "59963026-...",
  "name": "Steel production",
  "processType": "UNIT_PROCESS",
  "location": { "@type": "Location", "name": "Germany" },
  "exchanges": [ ... ]
}
Exchange — one input or output of a process:
{
  "@type": "Exchange",
  "internalId": 1,
  "amount": 1.0,
  "isInput": false,
  "isQuantitativeReference": true,
  "isAvoidedProduct": false,
  "flow": { "@type": "Flow", "name": "Steel" },
  "unit": { "@type": "Unit", "name": "kg" },
  "flowProperty": { "@type": "FlowProperty", "name": "Mass" }
}
Flow — a material, product, energy, or emission that moves between processes:
{
  "@type": "Flow",
  "name": "electricity, high voltage, at grid",
  "flowType": "PRODUCT_FLOW",
  "location": { "name": "Poland" },
  "flowProperties": [
    {
      "isRefFlowProperty": true,
      "flowProperty": { "name": "Energy" }
    }
  ]
}
Flow types are: PRODUCT_FLOW (technosphere), ELEMENTARY_FLOW (biosphere), or WASTE_FLOW.
UnitGroup — a family of related units with conversion factors:
{
  "@type": "UnitGroup",
  "name": "Units of energy",
  "units": [
    { "name": "MJ",  "isRefUnit": true,  "conversionFactor": 1.0 },
    { "name": "kWh", "isRefUnit": false, "conversionFactor": 3.6 }
  ]
}
ProductSystem — the full supply chain model:
{
  "@type": "ProductSystem",
  "name": "Ingot casting",
  "refProcess": { "name": "Ingot casting" },
  "refExchange": { "internalId": 1 },
  "targetAmount": 1.0,
  "targetUnit": { "name": "kg" },
  "processes": [ ... ],
  "processLinks": [ ... ]
}
ImpactCategory — one impact category with its characterisation factors:
{
  "@type": "ImpactCategory",
  "name": "Depletion of abiotic resources",
  "referenceUnitName": "kg antimony eq.",
  "impactFactors": [
    {
      "value": 1.09e-9,
      "flow": { "name": "Aluminium" },
      "unit": { "name": "kg" }
    }
  ]
}

Issue 1 — Unit groups are incorrectly structured
The product graph has a flat units dict:
units:
  kWh: Energy
  kg:  Mass
  L:   Volume
The script currently creates one UnitGroup per symbol. But in the olca-schema, a UnitGroup is a family of interconvertible units — for example, {kg, g, t, lb} all belong to one “Units of mass” group with conversion factors. The current approach creates orphaned single-unit groups that don’t match any real database’s unit structure.
This matters because when linking foreground processes to background processes, unit names must match exactly. If the background database uses a “Units of mass” group containing kg with a standard UUID, and our script creates a separate “Mass units” group also containing kg, openLCA may treat them as different units.
Recommended fix: replace the flat units dict with a reference to standard unit groups. Either hard-code the standard openLCA unit group UUIDs in the script, or look them up from the database at runtime before creating any flows.
Issue 2 — No flowType distinction for resources vs emissions
Both resources and emissions are ELEMENTARY_FLOW in the schema. The difference is directionality: emissions are outputs from the technosphere to the biosphere (isInput: false), resources are inputs from the biosphere to the technosphere (isInput: true). The product graph already captures this correctly via the emissions vs resources keys. No change needed — just confirming the mapping is right.
Issue 3 — No location field on flows or processes
Real background databases tag every process and product flow with a location (country or region). The product graph has no location field. For toy models this does not matter. For real-world LCA it will matter because ecoinvent process names include the location (e.g. "market for electricity, low voltage | DE"). The source: background field (to be added) should handle this by using the full database process name, which includes the location.





Before adding any new features, fix the way the script creates unit groups so they match the standard openLCA structure. The script should:

Check whether the required unit groups already exist in the database (by looking up standard names like “Units of mass”, “Units of energy”, etc.).
If they exist (because a real database has been loaded), use them by reference — do not recreate them.
If they do not exist (fresh empty database, toy model), create them with the correct multi-unit structure including standard conversion factors.

lcia_method: "ReCiPe 2016 Midpoint (H)"   # name of the method in the database
database:    "openlca-lcia-methods-2.1.2"  # documentary — which package was loaded

lcia_method is functional — the script looks up this method by name and passes it to CalculationSetup.
database is documentary — records which version of which data package was loaded, for reproducibility. Does not affect how the script runs.
Both fields are optional. If absent, the script runs inventory-only as today (backwards compatible).




# Look up method by name
methods = client.get_descriptors(o.ImpactMethod)
method  = next((m for m in methods if m.name == lcia_method_name), None)
if method is None:
    print(f"Warning: LCIA method '{lcia_method_name}' not found in database.")
    print("Running inventory-only. Load the LCIA methods package to enable impact scores.")

# Pass to calculation
setup = o.CalculationSetup(
    target=o.Ref(id=system_ref.id),
    amount=1.0,
    impact_method=method,   # None is safe — openLCA ignores it
)

# Retrieve impact results (Step 14)
if method:
    for impact in result.get_total_impacts():
        print(impact.impact_category.name,
              impact.amount,
              impact.impact_category.ref_unit)



## LCIA Results  (ReCiPe 2016 Midpoint H)

| Impact category        | Score    | Unit          |
|------------------------|----------|---------------|
| Climate change         | 6.40     | kg CO₂-eq     |
| Acidification          | 0.025    | kg SO₂-eq     |
| Eutrophication         | 0.0023   | kg PO₄-eq     |





Extend the product graph to allow processes to be declared as coming from a loaded background database rather than defined locally:
processes:
  - name: P1 — Cut and sew shirt
    source: local                    # defined in this product graph (default)
    reference_output: { flow: Shirt, amount: 1.0 }
    inputs:
      - { flow: Electricity, amount: 2.5 }

  - name: market for electricity, low voltage | DE
    source: background               # look up in the database by name
The script looks up background processes using:
provider = client.find(o.Process, "market for electricity, low voltage | DE")
and references them in the product system rather than creating them.
This requires a background process database to be loaded (US LCI, ELCD, etc.) — see Database Setup below.

Key insight: the unit process data tables shown in teaching slides (one table per process, with Name / Amount / Units / Type / Comments columns) are not the LCI result. They are the raw input data — equivalent to our product graph. The LCI result is produced only after solving the technology matrix (A × s = f) and multiplying by the intervention matrix (g = B × s). The LCI result contains only elementary flows (Emissions + Resources); all Intermediate and Technosphere flows cancel out algebraically and disappear.

All existing product graphs (coffee, cotton shirt, hand dryer, light bulb) explicitly model every upstream step — electricity generation is always its own process box. This means every entry in inputs has a matching reference_output somewhere in the same product graph and therefore counts as Intermediate, not Technosphere. No inputs are silently dropped from the diagram.
This is a deliberate pedagogical choice: making every step visible helps students understand the full supply chain. It is also why the diagram always draws correctly — every arrow has both a source and a destination within the product graph.
The Technosphere input distinction only becomes meaningful when background database support is added (see Step 3 below).







The olca-ipc Python client provides a method called create_product_system:
system_ref = client.create_product_system(
    process_ref,
    config=o.LinkingConfig(
        prefer_unit_processes=False,
        provider_linking=o.ProviderLinking.PREFER_DEFAULTS,
    )
)
This is openLCA’s auto-linking engine. When called, it:

Takes the reference (foreground) process as the starting point.
Scans every input of every foreground process for flows that have no supplier already defined within the foreground model.
Searches the entire database for any process whose reference output matches that flow (by flow name and unit).
If a match is found, links the background process into the product system.
Repeats recursively — the background process’s own inputs are also searched, pulling in further upstream processes until all inputs are satisfied or no more matches exist.

The result is a fully-linked ProductSystem object containing both the foreground processes (from the product graph) and any background processes found in the database.



The technology matrix A and the subsequent scaling vector s cover every process in the product system — foreground and background alike. If ecoinvent has 20,000 processes and auto-linking pulls in 5,000 of them to satisfy the apple supply chain, then A is a 5,000×5,000 matrix and s has 5,000 entries. openLCA handles this internally; the student only sees the final aggregated LCI and LCIA results.



If create_product_system finds no supplier for a Technosphere input (because no background database is loaded), that input is left unlinked. The product system is incomplete. The calculation still runs but the results are partial — the upstream emissions from electricity, fertilizer, diesel etc. are missing. The script should warn the user in this case.



Before auto-linking, you can ask openLCA what is available:
# Find every process in the database that produces a given flow
flow_ref = o.Ref(name="Electricity, low voltage")
providers = client.get_providers(flow_ref)
for p in providers:
    print(p.process.name)
    # e.g. "market for electricity, low voltage | DE"
    #      "electricity production, wind, <1MW turbine, onshore | DE"
This is useful for verifying that a background database is loaded and for letting the student choose which provider to use when multiple options exist.



The apple supply chain from the Constructing Inventories slides has 4 foreground processes (Production, Transport, Use, Disposal). Electricity, Fertilizer, Cardboard, Facility, and Diesel are Technosphere inputs to Production — they are NOT modelled as explicit process boxes in the product graph. The product graph would look like:
processes:
  - name: Production
    reference_output: { flow: Apple, amount: 500000, unit: kg }
    inputs:
      - { flow: Electricity, amount: 100000, unit: kWh }  # Technosphere — no local process
      - { flow: Fertilizer,  amount: 500000, unit: kg  }  # Technosphere — no local process
      - { flow: Diesel,      amount: 30000,  unit: kg  }  # Technosphere — no local process
    resources:
      - { flow: Water, amount: 100000, unit: L }
    emissions:
      - { flow: CO2 to air, amount: 100000, unit: kg }

  - name: Transport
    reference_output: { flow: Apple, amount: 5000, unit: kg }
    inputs:
      - { flow: Apple, amount: 5000, unit: kg }            # Intermediate — from Production

  - name: Use
    reference_output: { flow: Waste, amount: 0.1, unit: kg }
    inputs:
      - { flow: Apple, amount: 1.0, unit: kg }             # Intermediate — from Transport

  - name: Disposal
    reference_output: { flow: Disposed waste, amount: 0.1, unit: kg }
    inputs:
      - { flow: Waste, amount: 0.1, unit: kg }             # Intermediate — from Use
With a background database loaded, create_product_system would automatically find and link processes for Electricity, Fertilizer, and Diesel. Without one, those inputs would be unlinked and the results would be incomplete.

text:
The current run-lca skill and lca_analysis.py script build a complete product system in openLCA and run a calculation. However the calculation only returns raw inventory results — e.g. “0.1 kg CO₂ per cup”. It does not produce impact scores (GWP in kg CO₂-eq, DALYs, species-years, etc.) because no LCIA method is passed to the CalculationSetup.
In other words, the skill currently stops at Step 2 (Characterisation) of the LCIA chain. Steps 3 and 4 (damage modelling, endpoint scores) are not reached.

title: Plan: Adding LCIA Methods and Database Support to the run-lca Skill
text:
The product graph format was designed from scratch to be readable for students. That was the right goal — but it was written without systematically checking every field against the olca-schema (the actual data format openLCA uses internally). Before extending the product graph with new fields, we need to confirm that every existing field maps cleanly onto a real olca-schema concept, and identify any gaps or mismatches.
The olca-schema example files live at: https://github.com/GreenDelta/olca-schema/tree/master/examples



Every object in openLCA is a JSON file with a @type field, a UUID @id, and typed fields. Here are the key types relevant to the product graph:
Process — one production step in the supply chain:
{
  "@type": "Process",
  "@id": "59963026-...",
  "name": "Steel production",
  "processType": "UNIT_PROCESS",
  "location": { "@type": "Location", "name": "Germany" },
  "exchanges": [ ... ]
}
Exchange — one input or output of a process:
{
  "@type": "Exchange",
  "internalId": 1,
  "amount": 1.0,
  "isInput": false,
  "isQuantitativeReference": true,
  "isAvoidedProduct": false,
  "flow": { "@type": "Flow", "name": "Steel" },
  "unit": { "@type": "Unit", "name": "kg" },
  "flowProperty": { "@type": "FlowProperty", "name": "Mass" }
}
Flow — a material, product, energy, or emission that moves between processes:
{
  "@type": "Flow",
  "name": "electricity, high voltage, at grid",
  "flowType": "PRODUCT_FLOW",
  "location": { "name": "Poland" },
  "flowProperties": [
    {
      "isRefFlowProperty": true,
      "flowProperty": { "name": "Energy" }
    }
  ]
}
Flow types are: PRODUCT_FLOW (technosphere), ELEMENTARY_FLOW (biosphere), or WASTE_FLOW.
UnitGroup — a family of related units with conversion factors:
{
  "@type": "UnitGroup",
  "name": "Units of energy",
  "units": [
    { "name": "MJ",  "isRefUnit": true,  "conversionFactor": 1.0 },
    { "name": "kWh", "isRefUnit": false, "conversionFactor": 3.6 }
  ]
}
ProductSystem — the full supply chain model:
{
  "@type": "ProductSystem",
  "name": "Ingot casting",
  "refProcess": { "name": "Ingot casting" },
  "refExchange": { "internalId": 1 },
  "targetAmount": 1.0,
  "targetUnit": { "name": "kg" },
  "processes": [ ... ],
  "processLinks": [ ... ]
}
ImpactCategory — one impact category with its characterisation factors:
{
  "@type": "ImpactCategory",
  "name": "Depletion of abiotic resources",
  "referenceUnitName": "kg antimony eq.",
  "impactFactors": [
    {
      "value": 1.09e-9,
      "flow": { "name": "Aluminium" },
      "unit": { "name": "kg" }
    }
  ]
}

To add
Needed for real-world LCA using background databases






Issue 1 — Unit groups are incorrectly structured
The product graph has a flat units dict:
units:
  kWh: Energy
  kg:  Mass
  L:   Volume
The script currently creates one UnitGroup per symbol. But in the olca-schema, a UnitGroup is a family of interconvertible units — for example, {kg, g, t, lb} all belong to one “Units of mass” group with conversion factors. The current approach creates orphaned single-unit groups that don’t match any real database’s unit structure.
This matters because when linking foreground processes to background processes, unit names must match exactly. If the background database uses a “Units of mass” group containing kg with a standard UUID, and our script creates a separate “Mass units” group also containing kg, openLCA may treat them as different units.
Recommended fix: replace the flat units dict with a reference to standard unit groups. Either hard-code the standard openLCA unit group UUIDs in the script, or look them up from the database at runtime before creating any flows.
Issue 2 — No flowType distinction for resources vs emissions
Both resources and emissions are ELEMENTARY_FLOW in the schema. The difference is directionality: emissions are outputs from the technosphere to the biosphere (isInput: false), resources are inputs from the biosphere to the technosphere (isInput: true). The product graph already captures this correctly via the emissions vs resources keys. No change needed — just confirming the mapping is right.
Issue 3 — No location field on flows or processes
Real background databases tag every process and product flow with a location (country or region). The product graph has no location field. For toy models this does not matter. For real-world LCA it will matter because ecoinvent process names include the location (e.g. "market for electricity, low voltage | DE"). The source: background field (to be added) should handle this by using the full database process name, which includes the location.
